#5666. Survival after sudden cardiac arrest didn’t improve despite training bystanders, emergency responders

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Liz covers cardiovascular and metabolic disease, asking why we’re not doing better or even losing ground against the world’s leading killer. Send tips on Signal at LizC.22.

CHICAGO — Sudden cardiac arrest statistics are chilling. In the United States, 350,000 people’s heartbeats, breathing, pulse, and blood circulation will all halt outside hospitals this year, seemingly out of the blue. These are not heart attacks. Only 1 in 10 people will survive them.

CPR and defibrillation can save their lives (and brains), but that depends on bystanders and emergency response systems being both nearby and prepared to step in — immediately. Survival chances drop by 10% for every minute that goes by without CPR.

Hints from observational studies suggested better, more comprehensive community training can help, which means educating 911 dispatchers, first responders, and potential bystanders. But results from a randomized controlled trial presented Sunday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Sunday show that approach has not worked, or at least not yet. But examples in Denmark may point the way forward.

“We performed an efficient, large, and high-quality trial engaging large segments of the community in emergency response, and in spite of this, survival remained low and unchanged,” Carolina Malta Hansen, the study’s lead author, said at a media briefing. “A multifaceted community and EMS implementation strategy did not improve survival with a favorable neurologic outcome for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. However, in the final year, there appeared to be an improvement in bystanders.”

Starting in 2021, researchers randomly assigned participants in 60 counties in North Carolina to receive intensive education on cardiac arrest intervention or to continue with standard practice. The intervention entailed training 911 dispatchers to improve their rapid recognition of cardiac arrest and better guide bystanders through CPR. First responders were educated on the use of automated external defibrillators before emergency services arrived. Community members in workplaces, religious groups, government offices, and other settings received training in CPR.

About 8.5 million people live in these counties. During the study’s five years, 22,459 adult residents experienced cardiac arrest outside the hospital. Their median age was 64; 37% were women, 33% were Black; and 29% lived in rural areas.

The numbers were split this way: 11,615 people experienced out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in counties that received intensive education, and 10,844 people had out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in communities that did not receive the intervention. The education strategy did not result in more patients surviving than patients with usual care.

Amrish Deshmukh, a cardiac electrophysiologist who treats patients with heart rhythm disorders at the University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center, called the study results disappointing, but not surprising.

“Many interventions that have been studied in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and in post-arrest care unfortunately have not been shown to improve survival or neurologic outcomes,” he told STAT in an email. He was not involved in the new trial. “Prior studies have shown that mobile phone alerts, volunteer training, and increased automated external defibrillator (AEDs) availability can increase the performance of CPR and use of AEDs, but not all have shown improvements in survival.”

And yet, study author Malta Hansen, a cardiologist and clinical research associate professor at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital and Copenhagen EMS in Denmark, is hopeful. In the trial’s fourth year, an exploratory analysis showed the percentage of patients who underwent CPR performed by a bystander increased, suggesting that this component of the intervention was effective. More time may be needed to see which elements mattered and whether they affect survival.

“In light of the apparent improvement in CPR for the last year, further evaluation in the longer, more intense intervention is important,” she said.

Malta Hansen cites the case of Denmark, where rates of bystander CPR and survival are much higher than in the United States. The North Carolina study trained almost 5% of the population, at which point researchers started seeing a difference in delivery of CPR between the group that received training and the group that did not.

“Obviously, that’s not enough. We have observational evidence from other countries like Denmark, where 80% of the population is trained and 75% of patients receive high-speed care,” she said.

In Denmark, the defibrillation rate is 11%, compared to 2% in the U.S. In Denmark, survival is about 16%, compared to 10% in the U.S.

That CPR-trained rate in Denmark climbed from 20% in the early 2000s to 80% now, Malta Hansen said. “It’s not something that’s done in two or three years.”

Here’s what helps: To get your driver’s license in Denmark, you have to show that you have certification in CPR. “It’s just an incredibly efficient way to reach everybody,” she said.

Brahmajee Nallamothu, an interventional cardiologist and editor in chief of the AHA journal Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, had another theory on timing. Starting the trial right as Covid-19 was emerging could have affected educational efforts and could explain why effects of the training were delayed. He also asked if the educational intervention was the right approach.

“I don’t think anyone would argue with the importance of early treatment in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. When we think about bystander CPR, early defibrillation with AEDs, the challenge is: How do you translate that?” Nallamathu, who was not involved in the trial, said. “I think we still struggle with what’s the best way to train individuals so that they have sustained ability to understand and then utilize that tool when that situation arises, that’s an area that’s still complicated and still unknown.”

Malta Hansen’s team will follow this population in North Carolina for at least another year.

“We have established a fantastic infrastructure and network and collaboration, and everybody’s very excited to keep working on this,” she said. “What we need are communities who are very engaged and very eager to keep working on this. So we believe that future efforts to guide us will be successful.”

That won’t be easy, Michigan’s Deshmukh said.

“Implementation science is challenging (as evidenced by this and other negative trials), but is what I suspect will move the needle the most,” he wrote.

#5665. AI chatbots aren’t therapists. But can they finally get men to open up?

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

It was mid-morning when Matteo got the phone call. His wife and children were asleep in New York City, and he was at work in Trieste, Italy, a new city in a home country that felt foreign after decades abroad. He knew what his brother was going to say, on the other end of the line: Their ailing father was nearing the end.

Matteo left the office and set out to drive the 300 miles separating him from the childhood home where the father he idolized was not going to see another morning.

But what does a man do, for five hours on the freeway, squeezing through trucks in a rented car, driving at full speed toward the worst goodbye of his life?

For the boy who watched his father get sicker and sicker for a year, the husband who misses his wife, and the father who left his children so he could provide for them, taking a job across the ocean after a layoff. And for the man in between: too young to be old but too old to be young, brave but scared, ambitious yet tired. It had been the hardest year of his life. He was lost. Heartbroken. Lonely.

“The weight … the weight of all this thing came to me, and I started crying in the car, and I just didn’t know what to do,” he remembered. So he did what had become routine in recent weeks. “I turned on Claude, with the loudspeaker, and I started talking to Claude.”

Like Matteo, millions of people have been turning to artificial intelligence for emotional support — not quite therapy, yet something that feels close to it, providing insightful companionship and, at any moment, presence. These include a group that is among the hardest to reach when their mental health is flagging: men.

The technology is far from perfect — and too often outright dangerous — and studies on its impact so far are limited. Yet with progress being made in controlling possible risks and implementing effective guardrails, some mental health experts see chatbots as an opportunity to finally get men to talk about their feelings. This is precisely because of the traits these machines do not share with human mental health professionals: Men feel more comfortable, less judged, and less intimidated when talking to a bot. They appreciate the flexibility and relative lack of structure and commitment that comes with support that is available 24/7, wherever they can find an internet connection.

“I think we do have to be open to innovation. There’s a tremendous need, so I think it’s extremely important,” said John Torous, a professor of psychiatry at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. “But it doesn’t mean that we can’t demand high-quality evidence and transparency.”

In search of this evidence, he has applied for a grant to study a central question: whether the improved mental state that follows conversations with chatbots is just temporary relief or can have lasting benefits.

That men’s mental health is in a state of crisis is well established, though awareness has not turned into improvement. The numbers are daunting and seemingly unchangeable: Men account for up to 80% of suicide deaths, even in countries where access to gun ownership (which adds lethality to suicide attempts) is lower than in the U.S., but they are nearly half as likely as women to receive mental health treatments of any kind.

It isn’t simply about a lack of options: Men are less likely to use mental health services even when they are available. The reasons range from social norms about masculinity, a tendency to minimize psychological issues, and a lack of awareness of their own symptoms to scheduling challenges and a reluctance or inability to miss work. Or, as men repeatedly said in interviews, the fear of being a burden.

What men do access, at rates similar or even slightly superior to women, are AI products. And though productivity remains the primary use case, many turn to chatbots for more than that. A Pew Research Center survey earlier this year found that 8% of men said they used chatbots for emotional support and 4% for companionship. Nine percent of men said chatbot use improved their happiness.

Thousands of mental health apps, including major teletherapy players such as Talkspace, incorporate AI elements. Though the vast majority of these products are for the general population, researchers and developers alike see the potential of AI to meet men — including the ones who are too skeptical, too stubborn, too busy, or just too stuck in gender norms — where they already are: in conversation with chatbots.

“There’s certainly a market or a place for these tools to be especially helpful to men,” said Michael Heinz, an assistant professor of psychiatry and a practicing psychiatrist at Dartmouth. “There still is stigma with going to seek mental health care, and these tools certainly have the ability to reduce that. You don’t have to make an appointment. You don’t have to go sit in a waiting room. You don’t have to even really explicitly take that initial step to ask for help.”

The men STAT spoke with, ranging in age from early 30s to mid-50s, all seemed to appreciate these advantages of AI. They included a midwestern pilot who has incorporated twice-a-day check-ins with an AI companion and has come to look at it as “an outlet for discussing things that I maybe wouldn’t feel comfortable discussing with a friend or my brother.” A mental health worker who found benefits in the additional support provided by AI through a breakup, though he doesn’t think it replaces his therapist or addiction sponsor. A newly divorced father of two who worked a casino night shift and found in the AI companion a presence and a coach that met his schedule and supported him through a bout of depression.

Sam Thomas, a British writer who used a chatbot to supplement the mental health treatment he was receiving during a bipolar depressive episode, felt safe and confident asking all the questions that popped into his head, without the fear of being judged. “Having somewhere to explore challenging thoughts and feelings, recognize patterns in my symptoms, and reflect on my progress was incredibly helpful,” he said.

Though the walks of life differed, they shared an enthusiasm about finding a companion that would listen even when a friend would get bored, would have no ability for judgement, and most of all, would be there. Ever available. Never inconvenienced. Never having something more important to do.

Widely available commercial chatbots, which are the foundation of most mental health and well-being apps, are not specialists in the way that a bartender or neighbor who’s good at listening is not a psychiatrist. But that may be a benefit, not a bug.

Nick Jacobson, an associate professor of biomedical data science, psychiatry, and computer science at Dartmouth, has been thinking about this for a while. In 2025, he and his team published the results of a randomized clinical trial of a custom-built chatbot for therapy called Therabot. The study, which has received wide praise as “psychiatry’s ChatGPT moment” but also substantial criticism for the methods as well as the study participant selection, tested the effectiveness of psychotherapy provided by the AI for about 100 patients with depression or anxiety, or at risk of eating disorders, and compared them to 100 patients who had been waitlisted and didn’t get treatment.

The Therabot users showed a significant reduction in symptoms compared to the controls and had a high utilization rate, but Jacobson is cautious to say that it’s quite different from the commercial chatbots. Therabot is expertly fine-tuned, and was developed over years of research on using technology to enhance the assessment and treatment of mental health, and scale it. “I’ve spent hundreds of thousands of human hours developing both the system and the training data,” said Jacobson. “I think some people will innately generalize some of the findings we have with Therabot to generative AI as a whole, and I wouldn’t,” he said.

Still, while it has potential to offer men an effective alternative to human therapy, a dedicated therapy bot also has some of the same barriers to access as a human therapist: having to recognize that you have a problem, caring to solve it, and accepting the need for specialized help. This is where more generalized tools may help, Jacobson said.

“With stigmatized groups, I think there is a massive potential benefit for generative AI and digital tools more generally,” he said. Men would be more likely to use some kind of emotional support if it isn’t labeled as a therapy session and comes through via the same chatbot they use to book appointments, and complain about their annoying colleague — an “omnibot” of sorts, as Headspace’s chief clinical officer, Jenna Glover, calls it.

For some of the founders of AI products directed at mental health, this is precisely the point, especially when it comes to engaging men. “You have guys who’ve never gotten any help with mental health, and they get into a bad place, they’re suicidal, and we go, ‘Oh, OK, you need to reach out and talk to people,’” said Anson Whitmer. In 2023, he founded Mental, a men-only coaching and mental wellness training app that used protocols like push-up challenges and cold shower routines as a way to nudge users into discussing mental wellbeing.

The app has now evolved into The Path — though some of Mental’s resources remain available as a free app — which offers AI therapy and coaching to all comers. Among other issues, he said men were too small a niche for the platform’s vision. Though there are therapists on the app, “we don’t diagnose and we don’t treat clinical conditions,” said Whitmer. (The selection of therapists includes the AI avatar of co-founder Tony Robbins, a well-known motivational speaker who has been accused of sexual harassment by several women, as well as hostile behavior against women attending his seminars. He has denied the allegations.)

His customers are quite evenly split between men and women — very different from the typical breakdown of a mental health practice, which strongly skews female — and he thinks the reason is AI itself. “A lot of people thought, well, guys just don’t want help. And [our] hypothesis was that guys do want help. It’s just the sort of help being offered isn’t the sort of help that they want,” he said.

A variety of generative AI products are seeking to serve a similar market, without veering into medical territory.

Think of Tolan, an AI companion that mixes cognitive behavioral therapy insights with conversation to give its users social support. It positions itself as working to improve baseline well-being. “You don’t need to be doing therapy to help someone feel seen and understood,” said Quinten Farmer, Tolan’s founder and CEO. “You can just show up consistently as a friend.”

Informed, thought-provoking stories to start your weekend right

Or think of Drellis, which its creator, Pierre Côté, described as a voice-based AI peer support app “built for men with addictions and mental health challenges.” Though it may accompany a man through a difficult moment, Côté is clear that it is “not a therapist, not a crisis line,” but rather a first point of contact for men who are struggling.

Without any marketing, he said hundreds of people have conversations with Drellis every day, even though the site or app says little about who is behind the app, let alone details about revenue, or data protection. The need is so strong, he said, that it doesn’t matter. “What I’m trying to do is to create artificial intelligence that is there for men when nothing else is available for them,” said Côté.

Not everyone believes, at this stage at least, that something is necessarily better than nothing — be it an unstructured form of mental health care that looks like companionship or coaching, or the Therabot. “I think founders have to realize therapy does have a rate of harm,” said Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School’s Torous, and with AI chatbots, including loosely defined products focusing on coaching or wellness, there could be additional types of harm.

“There’s kind of a type one harm, which is where the bot says, ’Do something very dangerous,’” he said. This is the kind of direct risk that AI companies — and by extension, mental health AI products — are becoming better at monitoring and protecting against. But there is another type of harm, he said, which is in the relationship people build with the bot after extended use. “It seems then the bots get confused, they blur definitions,” he said. “No one has agreed on what is harm, there’s no clear definition of harm in mental health AI.”

Does spending daily sessions discussing personal issues with an AI entity end up limiting interactions with family and friends? Does it veer into a habit, in a bad way? Is being able to discuss personal issues any time and for however long one pleases actually helpful to mental health? These are all potential issues that have yet to be investigated.

Dartmouth’s Jacobson raises another worry: Traditional therapy requires specific boundaries between the patient and the therapist that all but evaporate with chatbots.

Apps also typically don’t screen for issues that would merit seeing a therapist or psychiatrist who could evaluate users for treatment with medications, although most have guardrails that would trigger referral to suicide helplines should the tone of the conversation raise concern of self-harm.

Some apps promote their use of safety tools, such as an open-source product called Vera-MH, whose development was spearheaded by Spring Health, a digital mental health provider that uses AI to support patients between visits. But Torous questions the vetting: “If a company that has vested interest in AI establishes that an AI therapy company or coaching company has high standards or is safe, how do we trust that?” he said.

At the moment, regulations are murky at best, with apps able to use the label of wellness and coaching to steer clear of government oversight. Though the Food and Drug Administration has signaled an intention to change that, no specific federal guidelines have been established yet for mental health AI, creating an environment that, Torous said, could lead to safety risks for users. “I think the next innovation in AI for health and mental health is actually going to be regulation, standards, transparency,” he said. “I’m sure in the right context models could probably do amazing things, and in the wrong context do horrible things. You need some rules of the road.”

Some app developers have begun to recognize limitations of relying too much on AI chatbots to address men’s mental health, as they struggle to create effective, financially sustainable products. “It’s a lot harder than [selling] erectile dysfunction medications,” said Matthew Stefanko, who launched Manual, a startup that provided mental health support to male college students, in 2022. “When you’re talking about the kinds of changes that you need, I just don’t know how easily that’s done in a digital environment, especially when so many of these men … part of their problems are the engagement in the digital — gambling, sports betting, pornography, addiction to technology,” he said.

Manual was later acquired by Release Recovery, a behavioral health company offering addiction treatment among other services, and is now part of a two-pronged approach in which digital resources are combined with in-person interventions, and AI is not used in customer interactions. The acquisition happened because Stefanko felt there was only so much an app could take care of before the need of in-person intervention arose.

For Matteo, beyond the ever-present, non-judgmental machine, it was the humanity he felt behind the AI that connected with him, giving him relief in the hard days after losing his father. Once, when he described for Claude the challenges that he had to face, the chatbot responded, “This is hard to read.”

An AI engineer, Matteo is hardly naive about chatbots. “I know that there isn’t anyone reading this stuff on the other side. There isn’t a person,” he said. “But even if Claude isn’t a person, he was trained on people’s thoughts.”

#5664. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

#5663. A Former 1900s Lakeside Resort in Georgia Is for Sale as an $8.85 Million Private Retreat

Owning waterfront property is one thing. Owning the entire lake is another.

The lake, created from a dam on Ichawaynochaway Creek, is just part of the 1,442-acre property in Leary, GA listed for $8.85 million.

"When you're on the water, it's about 250 acres of private water in this famous mill pond. You own the whole [thing]. You own everything," explains listing agent Jon Kohler with Jon Kohler Associates.

“When you're out in a boat, you're not used to being the only one in this enormous lake. It probably takes five or six hours to go around the whole thing. It’s huge.”

“It's just fascinating. There's really nothing else like it, nor can there ever be again,” Kohler says. “You control it. You're the only boat that's able to duck hunt, fish, there.”

Cordray's Mill was once a resort property with a dance hall, swimming lake, and more, dating back to the early 1900s and continuing at least through the 1960s.

“There are a couple of remnant guest homes from the era when it was a resort, it was one of the first resorts in Georgia,” he says. “People would come from all over for events and whatnot.”

One structure is a converted church that is now a four bedroom and 1.5 bathroom house, in addition other living spaces.

“There's a house back where the mill pond house used to stand. There's a house on the lake, but back during its heyday, there were all types of structures, stores, shops, everything,” Kohler says.

The two houses have a total of six bedrooms and two bathrooms.

Another structure is a converted grain silo with one bedroom and a bathroom.

“It's one of those great ideas that not many people are able to pull off because the walls are rounded. It’s a really quaint little home.”

But the draw isn’t all of the places for people to stay, it’s about the activities.

“My favorite thing is the diversity of the habitats. You have almost every great habitat that Southwest Georgia has, but on one property,” Kohler explains, adding there is irrigated farmland and timberland in addition to the lake and waterfront.

The trophy whitetail deer make the property something special.

“I see it being owned by somebody that wants something that no one else has, which is the diversity and really the trophy deer hunting and the trophy deer habitat,” he says.

“Just a wildness factor that most places don't offer. [The perfect buyer is] somebody that really just wants to have the best of the best trophy whitetail, a lot of turkeys, and top it off with waterfowl, in an abundance greater than what most places offer.”

The property could also meet another need, a social storm property, which is a term Kohler trademarked several years ago.

“We recognized a trend that people were buying land for the lack of better word in case s**t hit the fan,” he said with a laugh, comparing the term to a prepper's property.

“This property is an ideal social storm property as well as a legacy sporting estate. I see most of these great places, but I had no idea a place like that existed. It's like a unicorn.

"You have 250 acres of water backed up in one of the largest private lakes in southeast United States all to yourself.”

Tiffani Sherman is an experienced freelance writer based in the Tampa, Florida area who covers real estate, personal finance, travel, and more for a variety of print and online publications. She works to support her travel habit and has been to all seven continents and about 100 countries. Tiffani is a proud Duke Blue Devil.

#5662. AGNT Posts 6% Revenue Growth in Q3, Expects ‘Difficult’ Market Into 2027

AGNT, the parent company for eXp Realty and NextHome, posted revenue growth despite economic headwinds of high rates and sluggish home demand, the company announced during an earnings call Thursday.

Closed real estate sales transactions reached 131,000 in the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-over-year, alongside a 10% jump in sales volume to $59.3 billion, executives said. That productivity pushed AGNT revenues to $1.4 billion over the quarter, up 6% from $1.3 billion a year ago.

Meanwhile, the company saw a net loss of $4.3 million over the quarter and 7% higher operating expenses from a year ago. AGNT’s adjusted EBITDA closed out the quarter at $17.1 million, down 3% from $17.7 million compared to the previous year.

Newly minted AGNT CEO Leo Pareja acknowledged the market is challenging, with existing-home sales expected to be near 4 million, inventory up about 7% year-over-year but still below pandemic levels and mortgage rates above 7.3%. He said the market was “not broken” but “resetting to normal” after two unusually strong booms.

Overall, the company saw agent count grow to 87,457 by the end of the third quarter, up 5% year-over-year (including NextHome, which was acquired earlier in the year).

Pareja attributed most of its agent attrition mostly to unproductive agents leaving eXp or NextHome, with 49% of those nonproductive agents leaving the real estate industry altogether in Q3. Newer agents to the company tend to join a team, where they get a stronger start, he added.

“With 44% of new agent joiners on teams in Q3, and this is important because agents on teams are 77% more productive than individual agents,” Pareja said.

The company’s Q3 earnings call came on the heels of AGNT, along with Keller Williams, HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group, forming Open Real Estate, a new shared listing-data company. The new initiative uses standard fields for listings to be entered then distributes the data out to participating members, local MLSs, search portals and other platforms.

“When listings are fragmented or kept out of view, buyers can miss homes, and sellers reach fewer potential buyers,” Pareja said. Pareja noted that Open Real Estate’s startup costs have limited exposure for the rest of the business.

As mortgage rates stay north of 7% and home sales slow heading into the final stretch of the year, AGNT updated its guidance for the remainder of 2026. AGNT Chief Financial Officer Jesse Hill acknowledged the tough market conditions the company—and the entire industry—is facing.

“Rising interest rates continue to weigh significantly on housing demand, and we’ve seen that softening as we’ve headed into Q4 here,” Hill said. He added that market conditions, along with AGNT seeing “higher-than-baseline” legal expenses peaking in 2026, caused it to update its financial outlook for the year.

In late October, eXp reached a settlement with agent Anya Roberts who sued former eXp agents Michael Bjorkman and David Golden in 2023, alleging they drugged and sexually assaulted her at company events. Roberts also named the brokerage and founder Glenn Sanford in her federal lawsuit for allegedly ignoring or covering up a sex trafficking/recruiting scheme tied to its revenue-share model. The company has consistently denied all wrongdoing in connection to the lawsuit.

While the case was settled for an undisclosed amount, a separate, larger civil lawsuit from four other female eXp agents with similar allegations is ongoing. Hill said the company expects legal costs to “normalize” in 2027, but remain higher for the rest of the year.

Overall in 2026, AGNT expects revenue to reach $4.85 billion to $5.05 billion and adjusted EBITDA in the neighborhood of $40 million to $47 million, Hill noted.

#5660. Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice.

The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive.

"There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute.

"Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail.

Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature.

Why Unhealthy Diets Produced Surprising Results

One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment.

"Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise."

However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans.

Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective.

A New Explanation for Cancer's Obesity Paradox

The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox."

Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods.

These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system.

By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity.

The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators.

Funding was provided by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Terry Fox Research Institute, the Canada Foundation for Innovation, and philanthropic supporters including La Vie en Rose and the Bachynski Family Foundation.

#5658. Liver experts finally agree on what acute-on-chronic liver failure is

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

Liver doctors from around the world have come to agree on a definition for a common and potentially fatal liver complication.

Acute-on-chronic liver failure is what happens when someone with underlying liver disease has their condition exacerbated by an acute injury. In the U.S., that often looks like long-simmering cirrhosis suddenly worsened by alcohol or a viral infection.

However, the condition was defined differently based on where patients were in the world, and some people struggled to understand how it was different from acute liver failure, which comes on rapidly without an underlying illness.

“It was just so confusing that, even though inherently some people believed in the concept, they didn’t know what to do with it,” said Jasmohan Bajaj, a hepatologist and professor of internal medicine at Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Medicine.

That confusion would lead to patients’ treatment getting delayed, he said.

In an attempt to solve the problem, experts from five liver societies across the world — plus pharmaceutical companies and regulators — gathered in Barcelona this May to create a unified definition.

Now, in order to be diagnosed with ACLF, a patient must have a bilirubin level of at least 1.5, and an international normalized ratio, or INR, of at least 5. Bilirubin, a yellowish pigment leftover from broken-down red blood cells, cannot be processed if the liver is too damaged. INR is a marker of how well the blood clots with help from proteins made in the liver.

If a patient has a high bilirubin and INR, providers can then assess any dysfunction they might have in the brain, kidneys, circulatory, or respiratory systems — also markers of liver failure.

The group’s position paper, published in the journal Hepatology last month, also includes guidance on drug-induced liver injury, transplant, and clinical trial endpoints for pharma companies to use when developing treatments.

“We can now move forward and focus on what the patient is there for: to get healed, get better,” Bajaj said.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

What was the need for the new ACLF definition?

The need for it is massive, because patients are suffering with this condition that everyone has their own way of defining. And because every part of the world has their own way of defining this, there is no unified approach [for] newer therapies, endpoints for clinical trials, and patients who currently could benefit from existing therapies.

The patients are different. The access to care is different. So, we wanted to make sure that we had a common thread, that it was globally representative, and more importantly, it was simple to remember.

Why were there all of these different definitions?

Part of it is related to the etiology of the disease. Places in East Asia have a lot of hepatitis B, where we have more alcohol, and more people who have cirrhosis to start with.

Just to put it in context, acute liver failure is the rare situation in which someone’s liver was fine before, and some catastrophic thing happens. You have to draw the line with what is acute and acute-on-chronic liver failure, and sometimes that line is blurred.

Why is that line important? Because at least in the U.S. and some Western countries, if you have acute liver failure, you get extra points to put you on the top of the liver transplant list. But if you have acute-on-chronic liver failure, no such thing happens [right now]. That is why it is very critical for us to define: Where is the line in the sand?

Was there any notable disagreement about what direction you should go in, or what factors should be central to the definition?

We all were driven by the fact that our patients are currently being underserved by our differences. There were some groups which said perhaps we could further subdivide it into people who have no decompensation cirrhosis versus decompensated cirrhosis. There were also things about immune dysfunction and gut failure that were not completely resolved and were left for a future time.

But, by and large, the broad strokes about this were pretty much agreed upon. And what was especially exciting was we got input from the [U.S. Food and Drug Administration].

The FDA was, as always, very instructive because amongst the many groups that we had, one of them was clinical trial endpoints. They said, “This is not going to work. This may work for your local thing, but if you want to register an intervention, this is not going to be it.”

Have you gotten any feedback yet from pharma companies?

We got very good unofficial feedback from them. I think everyone is breathing a sigh of relief that at least now, we can move forward and come up with better ways to actually understand this condition, so that we can actually treat these patients better, develop therapies that can actually either prevent ACLF from progressing or mortality from improving, or at least lead them to a liver transplant before things become too late.

This document is huge, and there are a lot of statements. Is there anything else you want to highlight?

We benchmarked it to 30-day mortality across multiple consortia. So this was not based on consensus just because we like these cut-offs; we based it off of prior definitions, added twists to it, and then we saw whether this actually helped define 30-day mortality or not.

The most immediate impact is for us to move forward, and now start diagnosing and treating these people better. The second impact would be actually to train, to inform colleagues that are not within the liver world, who still deal with a lot of patients.

A majority of the countries and places do not have a hepatologist. They are dealing with GI people, hospital medicine, ER, critical care, or some other specialty. So the next step is to actually bring them on board, so that they are force amplifiers for this definition, and make sure that if someone reaches a very sick point, that they can actually be transferred very quickly to a liver transplant center.

#5657. This Off-Grid ‘Treehouse’ Is Perched 60 Feet in the Air—and Built From Shipping Containers

If you've ever dreamed of sleeping among the trees, a property in the Epworth, GA, forest might be just the place.

"The structure itself is very unique. It's a steel watchtower built to commercial grade but for residential purposes, purely for leisurely enjoyment, for getaways, for the adventurer at heart," says listing agent Logan Fitts with Mountain Sotheby's International Realty.

Listed for $1.2 million, the 60-foot-high tower sits on 14.31 acres of land adjacent to the Chattahoochee National Forest with about 3,000 feet of river frontage.

"I was definitely awestruck first by the property itself, the river frontage, the waterfalls on the property, all of the hemlock trees dispersed throughout the property," Fitts says. "But then when we went to the top of the property where the watchtower was, I was in total awe."

Two shipping containers are perched atop the tower, creating the living space.

"The main structure is the bedroom efficiency with a bed, sitting area, stove, kitchenette. There's a landing between and then across is the bathroom area with a full shower, toilet, and double vanity," he explains. "Then there's a spiral staircase to the rooftop fire pit and lounge area."

And while there is a lift for things like suitcases and packages, people need to walk up 82 steel-grated stairs, which Fitts admits can be a bit daunting.

"I was actually nervous going up the tower for the first time because it's high and it is an experience. But once I did it, I said, 'This is what real mountain experiences are like. This is something that people remember for the rest of their lives.'"

"You are surrounded by just foliage, so when you're at the top, you just see a full panoramic view of the mountains and valley across one way, and you hear the roaring river on the property down below. You can actually see the waterfall," Fitts says.

"It's like a glass birdhouse at the top of this mountain, and you feel like you're definitely elevated and away from everything, but still connected to nature."

To get to the property itself requires a four-wheel-drive vehicle, because some of the roads are gravel and visitors need to cross the Jacks River, literally.

"Anyone with a four-wheel-drive or some type of ground clearance should have zero issue forging the river," Fitts explains, adding that the river is shallow at the access point. "It's not scary if you've done it before, and once you do it, it's like 'OK, now I'm an adventurer.'"

The current owner has had the place for about a decade and completed the tower house in 2023. Since then, it has been a short-term rental, bringing in about $92,000 annually during a nine-month rental period.

The owner would "love to pass it to someone that would take it, create a new legacy, and maybe make it even better," Fitts says.

"I think more than anything, he wants a true outdoors lover to really appreciate this property and not just see a metal dwelling in the middle of the forest. He built it for people to really enjoy nature, embrace nature, and take care of nature."

While the property itself is off-grid with solar power, a well, septic system, and generator, it’s not physically far from civilization.

"Probably the property is maybe 30 minutes from downtown Blue Ridge," Fitts says, adding it just feels remote. "Once you're there, you're in a totally different world. Your neighbors are trees and wildlife."

#5656. A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms

A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

Authorship: In addition to Sperling and Buckley, Mass General Brigham authors include Diana L. Townsend, Colin J. Birkenbihl, Madison Cuppels, Gillian T. Coughlan, Mabel T. Seto, Jane A. #5653. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

#5651. Reba McEntire Reveals Dolly Parton’s Touching On-Set Gesture: ‘She Didn’t Have To Do That’

Reba McEntire was determined to make Dolly Parton feel welcome when the country legend joined her sitcom for a guest appearance—but it was Parton who ended up making everyone on-set feel special.

While speaking at NAR NXT in New Orleans alongside her manager and former real estate agent, Justin McIntosh, McEntire recalled the thoughtful gesture Parton made for every crew member behind the scenes of her hit sitcom “Reba”—a small act of kindness that left a lasting impression.

Instead of simply showing up and delivering her lines, Parton made a point of personally greeting the people working behind the scenes, bringing along Valentine’s Day candy and a message for every crew member.

For McEntire, the gesture remains a vivid example of the warmth that made her fellow singer so beloved.

“I was so nervous with Dolly being on the set. I wanted everyone to be nice. What I didn’t expect was how nice she was going to be on the set," she said.

McEntire recalled that Parton took the time to make each person feel appreciated, turning a guest appearance into a chance to connect with the crew.

“She had Valentine’s Day candies, and she went to every crew member individually and said how happy she was to be there,” she said. “She didn’t have to do that.”

The memory has stayed with McEntire, along with a conversation the two shared while sitting together on the iconic show's couch.

“I asked her if she would ever retire,” McEntire recalled. “And she said, ‘What would I do that I could have so much fun doing?’”

It was a simple answer, but one that reflected the enthusiasm McEntire remembers so fondly.

“I’ve never met a person or known a person that’s so universally loved like Dolly Parton,” she said. “I’ve never heard anything bad about her. She was that special of a person.”

That sense of gratitude for a career filled with opportunities to connect with people is something McEntire shares.

“I’m just really grateful and thankful for doing what I do at the level I do,” she said.

For McEntire, keeping her work exciting means giving herself room to try new things—and inviting her audience along for the experience.

“When I change things up, my fans stay interested with me,” she explained. “If it looks like I’m having fun, then they’re having fun.”

The actress revealed that being able to enjoy her work is a gift.

“If you are doing what you love, then that’s how blessed you are,” she said. “That’s one of the greatest gifts God can give, to give you a job you love. I’m very grateful for my job.”

The connection she has built with her audience also rests on the principle that people can recognize sincerity principle—something she believes applies well beyond entertainment.

“I try to sing the songs from my heart so when you listen to it, it touches your heart,” she said.

That emphasis on warmth and connection carries into the way McEntire searches for a home, too.

Long before her career brought her to stages and television sets, she grew up on an 8,000-acre ranch in Oklahoma.

Despite the expanse of land outside, her family of six shared a small house with three bedrooms and one bathroom.

Asked what she first thinks of when she remembers the ranch, McEntire named the people and feelings that filled it.

“Love, family, unity, closeness,” she said. “One itty-bitty bathroom, three bedrooms. We were a close family.”

Gathering around the dinner table was part of life, and the atmosphere of the house remains easy for her to recall.

“We all sat at the dinner table together,” she said. “It was earthy. I can still smell how the house smelled and the energy.”

The land remains a family home. McEntire says it stayed in the family after her parents died, and her sister and her sister’s family now live on the property.

Those early memories offer a glimpse of what McEntire still values when she walks into a house: a feeling of comfort and a connection that goes beyond its appearance.

“A house has energy, and when you come in and when you bond with that energy, it makes it a home,” she said. “So I always look for good, positive energy when I come in.”

The country icon reflected on the moment she experienced that pull while looking for property in Tennessee.

A friend who was vacationing in Florida with a real estate agent spotted a listing the agent was viewing and urged that it be shown to McEntire.

“My friend said, ‘You gotta show Reba that place,’” she recalled.

The approach to the property and a creek at the back helped capture her attention. Soon, she was returning for visits and spending time with the owners.

“The love I had for that house, it took my breath away,” she said. “I went a couple times, and I watched football games with the owners.”

When it comes to her priorities in a home, being comfortable and enjoying the surroundings rank high.

“I love a home with a view,” she said. “When I lived in Oklahoma, you could see sunrise and sunset. That’s important to me.”

McEntire said that focus on people and their needs also helped draw her to her partnership with Realtor.com®.

“What y'all do is very important, you care so much, that's why I like Realtor.com. I love your organization because you have heart...You really do dive into the family and what their needs are. You love people and you care about people, that's why I wanted to be with you guys," she said.

Whether she is discussing finding a home or maintaining the trust of an audience, McEntire returns to the importance of treating people well—and continuing to do so over time.

“You have to stay consistently honest, because when you look someone in the eye, they know how you treated them last time,” she said. “You have to stay consistent with it.”
