#5626. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

#5625. Meet the 27-Year-Old Who’s Trying To Bring Housing Back to Rural Ohio

When it comes to the hottest locations that attract young 20-somethings, Mansfield, OH, probably isn't the first place that comes to mind.

For years, Mansfield’s nickname was “The Fun Center of Ohio” because of its family-friendly attractions and its status in the 1970s as a mini-bike manufacturing hub.

More recently, the town of 47,000, located halfway between Columbus and Cleveland, earned the local nickname of “Danger City” after the Westinghouse electric plant left in 1990 and the town fell into deep economic decline.

The 27-year-old serial entrepreneur, who started a painting and landscaping business as a teenager, relocated to Mansfield from Seattle a year ago, hoping to revitalize rural housing through his vertically integrated housing development company, Western Dominion Land.

Vertical integration is a development model in which a single company controls the full life cycle of a housing project.

“In other countries, they’ve figured out that vertically integrating construction means you’re not paying a margin out to every single step," Goehner explains. "If you own the system—from a lumberyard, to producing panels or modular, to buying the land, to developing the land, to building the homes—you're not paying everyone’s markup along the way, and you can actually deliver that home at a reasonable price.”

Goehner is building a factory in Mansfield to produce structured panels that he says will cut single-family home construction from months to weeks and allow him to charge much less than other builders. The first panels are expected to roll off the production line in early 2027.

Currently, it takes 8.8 months to construct a home from start to finish, according to the National Association of Home Builders. Goehner says his process allows a home to be built and move-in-ready in 40 days.

Western Dominion has already built about 500 housing units across Ohio, starting at $200,000 for a single-family home.

Western Dominion focuses on what it calls "attainable housing"—homes priced below what the median household income in the area can afford but not income-limited, meaning they work for the vast majority of families and buyers.

In Mansfield, where the median listing price is $229,000, he says, "single-family homes at $215,000 sold instantly. At $260,000, they sat for months."

As he sees it, 25% of the homes on the market are priced for 60% to 70% of buyers, while the rest of what’s being built is at the top end of the market. Furthermore, only 8% of construction happens in rural areas, despite 20% of the population living there.

"The government is too focused on low-income housing" and low-income housing tax credits, he says. “And the last few housing bills they passed were only structured to deliver essentially more urban multifamily units and incentivize builders to build more low-income housing with tax credits."

In rural communities, he adds, “We have a terrible amount of aged housing inventory. Most of our homes are from before 1970, which would be fine if it didn't cost so much to remodel.

“From the '90s to the 2000s, we’re building a good amount of homes. As a country, we were doing about 1.6 million a year. And then in rural America, we were doing about 220,000 homes a year. And then 2008 hits, and that drops down to about 60,000 homes a year in rural America."

Along the way, smaller builders disappeared, and larger builders were disincentivized from building in rural areas because of the red tape involved.

"If you want to build in rural America and you go to a bank, unless you have all the cash, you have to show comps," he says. "You've got to be, like, ‘All right, we think these homes are going to sell for this much because these guys sold for this much.' And if no one's built for five to 50 years, which is the case in a lot of these communities, that can be difficult."

The added costs of building in rural areas, like having to pull utilities, "mean you're spending $25,000 to $50,000 per lot before you can even start putting a house on it or connecting your utilities to the lot."

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, home prices in rural communities have risen sharply. A Realtor.com® housing analysis of home prices from November 2019 to November 2025 found that median listing prices increased more than 70% in rural counties while in-metro counties saw home prices increase around 30% during the same time period.

"A lot of the politicians we talk to, they go, 'I didn't know that that county needed housing. I didn't know rural needed housing because the population is shrinking.' But then when you look at why the population is shrinking, it's because they haven't gotten any new homes for 20 to 40 years."

"You've got this huge demand. But on paper, on the surface, it looks like there's no demand because the population's declining," he continues. "And that's how you get cities like Holiday City."

Holiday City, near the Ohio border with Indiana and Michigan, has a population of just 48 people, but it is home to three large businesses—Chase Brass & Copper Co., 20/20 Custom Molded Products, and a Menards Distribution Center—which draw around 1,500 commuters from out of state.

"Let's put up, you know, 300 homes, and a portion of the workforce can actually stop commuting an hour or two every day," Goehner says.

Goehner hopes Ohio's new slate of elected officials will help advance rural building by offsetting some of the infrastructure-related costs of building in rural areas. In exchange, he would sell homes at his “attainable” housing rates.

"The government needs to stop spending thousands of dollars a month per unit to subsidize rents when they could simply spend a little bit upfront to make it viable to build at a reasonable price point again," he says.

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5624. Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think

Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age.

Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually.

The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions.

To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years.

Higher BMI Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time.

The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects.

Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years.

"We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well."

How Excess Weight May Affect the Aging Brain

Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities.

Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure.

Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%.

Weight Management Could Help Protect Brain Health

The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050.

Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.

"There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it."

The research was published in the Journal of Neurology. Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study.

#5622. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

#5621. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5620. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

#5619. Two Neighboring $9.9 Million Oceanfront Homes Just Listed in Kauai’s South Shore—And They Can Form an Ultra-Luxe Compound

Tucked into a private-club community in Hawaii called Kukui‘ula, two luxury homes just hit the market on Kauai's South Shore.

Set right on the ocean, and set among lush tropical vegetation, this walkable community is only 25-minute drive from Lihue Airport.

"The close proximity of everything is very convenient. You’re not having to spend a lot of time in the car,” says Pancho Sullivan of Hawaii Life, who is co-listing the two homes with Haunani Sullivan as well as Suzanne Harding and Jeff Skinner of Kukui‘ula Realty Group. The asking price sits at $9,900,000 each.

Both were built in 2025 and have never been occupied. Aepo Nei 18 and Aepo Nei 19 are neighboring 3,372-square-foot homes with four bedrooms and 4.5 baths each. They can be purchased together, to create a private compound, or by separate buyers.

Even better, the homes are fully furnished and stocked with items like bed and bath linens, beach towels, and everything you need to cook and serve in the kitchen, such as bowls, plates and glasses.

But it’s the design by Brazil-based Architects+CO that’s truly unique. Kauai Bahia Construction and their in-house material company, Kayu, handled all of the finish material production and millwork installation.

"Brazil is known for incredible resort-club communities," says Pancho. "We actually traveled to Brazil to look at some of the clubs they designed. It’s the same tropical feel (as Hawaii) that blends in really well with nature."

Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions while Aepo Nei 19’s living spaces open onto a lawn courtyard. Design features at both include deep roof overhangs, walls of glass and multiple outdoor living spaces such as an infinity-edge pool; jacuzzi; swim-in, swim-out sauna; and in-water fire pit.

"They both have beautiful 180-degree ocean views looking across the Tom Weiskopf-designed golf course. The swim-in, swim-out dry sauna facing the ocean is a unique feature," says Pancho, adding that the usage of natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak "fit into the landscape very beautifully."

Referred to as the Garden Island, Kauai is home to about 73,000 people.

"We get the majority of the island’s sunshine down here," says Haunani, about the South Shore. "People flock here for the beaches and the sunshine, Hawaiian monk seals on the sand, and a lot of ocean activity including surfing.

"A lot of people that venture to Kauai are adventure seekers. We have great hiking. You can get on a boat and dive on the Nā Pali Coast and do ziplining and ATV tours."

Stand-up paddleboarding, diving and fishing are two other activities easy to do in this community.

Homeowners become club members with access to dining, a pool, spa (boasting a steam rook and lava-rock dry sauna), pickleball and tennis courts, and an 18-hole golf course.

"There’s an incredible gym with classes daily, from yoga to sound bathing to fitness training," says Pancho. "All of that is part of your club membership. It’s a great place to be in tune with nature and get healthy."

A 10-acre organic garden features a farm stand as well as opportunities to create floral bouquets. There’s also a conscious effort to honor Hawaiian history through cultural-heritage walks; sunrise ceremonies; hula performances; and classes in Hawaiian featherwork, quilting and basket weaving.

“Members who are part of the club become life-long friends,” says Haunani. “They’re going to each other’s second homes and weddings. They travel around the world together.”

The community also organizes annual golf and pickleball tournaments for members, and three golf courses are within a seven-minute drive.

Another incentive is that the community’s zoned as a Vacation Destination Area.

This means properties can join the short-term rental pool, for minimum seven-night stays.

"Some of the owners put their homes in the rental pool and block out time for themselves and their families. That’s a great added benefit," says Haunani, as few club communities on Kauai allow this.

The Sullivans think the buyer will likely hail from the West Coast, enticed by a direct flight from hubs in cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix and Denver that arrive on the island by mid-day.

“Kukui‘ula is a great place for families to gather and spend time together. We see a lot of members bring their entire families so they can vacation together multiple times per year,” says Pancho.

“With all these activities it’s easy to curate an incredible vacation with the convenience of being on property. A lot of people enjoy coming here and decompressing.”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5618. Housing Week Ahead: Hottest Markets, Inflation, and Existing-Home Sales

The coming week brings a steady stream of new reports from the Realtor.com economics team, as well as a number of key indicators for the housing market.

On Monday, senior economist Anthony Smith published the October Luxury Report, which looks at pockets of growth where luxury prices are still rising.

On Tuesday, ahead of Veterans Day, we honor America’s military service members and veterans with a report on Veterans Affairs loans. Senior economist Jiayi Xu explores what they are and how they help with homeownership.

On Wednesday, senior economist Hannah Jones examines how the lock-in effect has evolved and where today’s homeowners with a mortgage face larger or smaller payment shocks if they are thinking about moving.

On Thursday, Hannah is back to examine what the first full week of November data reveals about the housing market, and on Friday, Hannah publishes the October Hottest Markets report, which identifies the markets where homes are moving the fastest and getting the most attention from online shoppers.

Turning to the economic indicators that will be released, we’ll see the consumer price index reading on inflation as well as mortgage rates and existing-home sales.

Inflation has run above the Fed’s target, 2% growth in headline PCE, for 5.5 years, and it’s clear from exit polls that the cost of living was very much on the mind of voters in last week’s election.

This week, we’ll see the first inflation reading for October from the consumer price index, which was up sharply in September largely due to higher energy prices. I’m expecting the annual inflation reading to be similarly high in October even if the month-to-month momentum wanes a bit.

Although inflation remains elevated, mortgage rates could continue to ebb. Last week the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, according to Freddie Mac, dropped to 7.18% as the 10-year hovered near 4.9%.

Late in the week, the 10-year yield dropped further as uncertainty over artificial intelligence investments led to a pullback in stocks. Even if the 10-year were to remain at 4.9%, it has adjusted faster than mortgage rates, so I think there is room for spread compression that could help nudge rates lower, which will help late-season home shoppers.

The last indicator of the week is existing-home sales data from the National Association of Realtors®. That October home sales data is likely to be very disappointing.

Mortgage rates rose sharply in the month, and NAR’s pending home sales hit a series record low in September, while Realtor.com housing data suggests that the buyer pullback continued into October. I’m watching to see if the pullback is sufficient to push months supply even higher.

For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research.

Danielle Hale is the chief economist of Realtor.com.

The American Real Estate Association (ARA) on Nov. 9 announced that SERHANT., founded by celebrity agent Ryan Serhant, famous for his Manhattan-based reality TV show, has joined the national trade association.

Since expanding beyond New York in 2023, SERHANT. has grown to 20 states and Washington, D.C., including 2026 launches in California, Texas, Colorado, Massachusetts and Illinois.

ARA, according to a release, is focused on elevating professional standards and the value real estate agents deliver to the public. The release touted Serhant’s brand and global media network, claiming more than 11 million followers, as something that helps expand ARA’s national footprint and strengthens its platform.

“When we launched ARA, our mission was clear: build a unified voice of reason, an association by agents, for agents, that relentlessly fights for the industry,” said Jason Haber and Mauricio Umansky, co-founders of ARA, in a joint statement. “Attaching Ryan Serhant and SERHANT. into this mission is a major step forward. It shows that this industry belongs to true professionals who are fiercely dedicated to their clients and to delivering the highest level of service.”

Asked if ARA is also seeking out partnerships with smaller brokerages or getting involved in other local/state advocacy outside of New York and Missouri, Haber told RISMedia that “we are hearing from many smaller firms in the Midwest, as an example, and we are just as excited to meet with them as we were to meet with SERHANT. Not every firm will make headlines by signing up with us, but we are thrilled to work with them as well.

“There is clearly a hunger, excitement and enthusiasm across this country for a new voice in the industry. In November alone we rolled out our State Chair program, our licensee-in-the-loop legislation and our AI taskforce. Later this month we are giving back to the community by feeding 3,000 people for Thanksgiving. It’s a big month for us at ARA.”

Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT., as well as a broker, author and the star and executive producer of Netflix’s “Owning Manhattan,” said that “ARA is doing the hard work to raise the bar for the entire profession while fighting for homeownership across the country. Aligning SERHANT. with ARA gives our agents an even stronger platform to educate consumers, advocate for clients and shape where this industry goes next.”

“The rapid convergence of industry leaders under ARA’s umbrella shows how hungry the market was for modern, agent-first leadership,” said Briggs Elwell, co-founder and CEO of RLTYco and a member of ARA’s board of directors. “Pairing ARA’s advocacy and education with powerhouses like SERHANT. empowers agents to operate as true, highly skilled business owners.”

SERHANT. joins Compass International Holdings, REMAX and Douglas Elliman among the major firms that have aligned with ARA. This year the association expanded its board of directors with Chris Lim, the former president and chief growth officer of REMAX, and investor Andrew Dodge, who serve alongside Douglas Elliman President and CEO Michael Liebowitz, Douglas Elliman General Counsel Deva Roberts and Elwell.

ARA also continues to bring national weight to state fights. In August, Missouri voters rejected Amendments 4 and 5, ballot measures ARA opposed alongside the Missouri Association of Realtors®.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5616. Luxury Home Prices Are Falling, but These Pockets of Growth Are Defying the Slump

Luxury home prices are sinking in much of the country, but there are significant exceptions, where high-end home prices just keep rising.

The national threshold for luxury homes—defined as the top 10% of listings—in October came in at $1,197,014, down 2.3% from one year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly luxury report.

The downward trend held in the upper tiers of the luxury market, with the 95th percentile down 4.1% to a threshold of $1,873,040 and the 99th percentile down 6.2% to $5,125,874.

However, in certain golden pockets, the luxury market is thriving. Of the 43 metros in the report's dataset, 12 posted a year-over-year increase of 1% or higher.

"Although the price point for entry luxury has had 31 consecutive months of annual decline at the national level, there are markets where prices are climbing and, in some cases, well above the year-ago levels," says the report's author, Realtor.com senior economist Anthony Smith.

Of those 12 robust luxury markets, the South massively dominates, with five markets in Florida alone. Only two Northern metros—Atlantic City and Detroit—made the cut.

Nor are these necessarily the most expensive markets in the U.S. While those pricey markets—with familiar names like Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury, CT, and Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, CA—have the highest entry thresholds to luxury, their prices are slipping.

Of the 12 most expensive markets, only Naples-Marco Island, FL, with an entry threshold of $3,753,333, continues to show price gains. Nor are these gains negligible—the metro's luxury threshold is up a very healthy 9.0% year over year.

While this is only 1.3 percentage points over second-place finisher North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota, FL, with a much lower entry to luxury at $1,796,850, it is a full 4.3 percentage points over third-place finisher Charleston-North Charleston, SC.

Naples comes ahead in another key way, too. Luxury properties are moving a median 27 days faster than last year, or 21.1% quicker, by far the fastest pace increase of all the growth metros. The second-place finisher, Cape Coral-Fort Myers, FL, is moving 18 days faster than last year, or 16.1%.

The price gains aren't limited to entry-level luxury, or the top 10%. Eight of the 12 metros saw all three luxury tiers rise from a year ago, a sharp contrast with the national picture, where all those thresholds fell.

The largest gain for the top 1% of listings (ultraluxury) came from Charleston-North Charleston, SC. Here, the entry-level luxe threshold rose 4.7% (the third-highest in the nation), but its top 1% of properties blasted past that with a median price increase of 18.7%, for a threshold of $8,044,460.

These are the top 12 growth markets for entry-level luxury:

North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota, FL (up 7.7%)

Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach, FL (up 4.1%)

Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (up 3.6%)

Las Vegas-Henderson-North Las Vegas, NV (up 2.2%)

Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater, FL (up 2.1%)

On the southwestern edge of the Sunshine State, dubbed the Paradise Coast, Naples has long lured snowbirds eager to escape Northern winters and embrace the blue-green waters and white sandy shores of the Gulf.

But it hasn't always been a top luxury haven; in fact, that aspect of the area is rather new.

Luxury broker Taylor Canada of Gulf Coast International Properties, who was born and raised in Naples, says that in the 1980s, the town was "nothing."

"On the beach, there were like four buildings," he tells Realtor.com.

But over the decades, the agent has seen the metro change dramatically, with booming development and sprawling Tuscan-style mansions and high-end retail. Still, the town has managed to retain much of its "small town" charm, thanks to tight building regulations.

"They are really trying to make it not Miami," he says of the city. "That attracts a lot of affluent buyers to the lifestyle and the quietness."

The wealthy in Palm Beach County are "more showy," he says. "Here, you could be behind a billionaire in the grocery store and never know."

The broker, who currently represents a $9 million, four-bedroom, 4.5-bath 5,000-plus-square-foot estate in Old Naples, isn't surprised that his hometown is bucking the national trend, with luxury prices on the rise.

"We're seeing records broken monthly," he says of certain exclusive and waterfront neighborhoods. Even the luxury condo market, which he says "struggled for a few years," is showing signs of a recovery, with the occasional bidding war.

Buyers at this level are the usual suspects, hailing from more expensive states such as New York, Washington, and California. But, uniquely, the area also sees a lot of local buyers who "shuffle around" from one luxury property to another.

"Every three to five years, they figure out where they want to go next," Canada says of mobile Naples lovers. "They go, 'Oh, maybe I want to be on the water, or maybe I want to get closer to the beach, or maybe I want to be in a golf community.'"

And while Naples still draws an older crowd, the agent says it is more common now to see buyers "in their 40s and their families." While the techies tend to head to Miami and the West Coast, the CEOs and business leaders prefer the East Coast, he says.

And what they want are properties that are brand-new, turnkey, and furnished.

"They're willing to pay a premium for that," he adds.

Florida's plethora of tax breaks—including the newly approved measure that would reform the state's property tax system—is luring high net worth individuals more than ever before.

"The tax break is paying for their property, almost," he says.

The metro with the second-highest annual growth in the nation, with a 7.7% increase, is 120 miles north of Naples, nestled along Sarasota Bay. Luxe homes, with an entry threshold of $1,796,850, are moving nine days faster than they did last year.

The North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota metro encompasses multiple barrier islands, including Longboat Key and Siesta Key, with famous Siesta Beach, which often tops "beat beaches" polls due to its nearly 100% quartz-crystal sand.

Like Naples, Sarasota wasn't always a luxury haven.

Local broker Joel Schemmel of Douglas Elliman has been representing the area for 25 years and concentrates on the top 1% of properties, or those over $4 million.

Those with fat pocketbooks began pouring into Sarasota during the COVID-19 pandemic, he says. Now, buyers continue to be lured by the pristine white beaches, cultural attractions (Sarasota has a vibrant arts community), and top-notch schools, including the renowned IMG Academy sports prep school in Bradenton.

"We've really seen movement in the ultraluxury market," he tells Realtor.com, noting that sales priced at $4 million and over are up about 80% since last year.

The broker attributes the soaring luxury market to the end of a buying funk, when people were "thinking a bit more" about investing in waterfront properties due to storms. In fall 2024, Sarasota County had just caught its breath from Hurricane Helene when it was slammed by Hurricane Milton.

But apparently those hurricane hesitations have been swept away.

"Newer construction went through the storms unscathed," says Schemmel. "All of those people who were on the fence are like, 'If I want a house in Florida, why not buy now?'"

The typical multimillion-dollar estate buyer is already familiar with the area and upgrading, says the broker. Then there are the out-of-towners—mostly from the New York-New Jersey-CT tristate area—who are discovering Sarasota for its comparable affordability.

"We have a lot more waterfront options, and our price point is in a different zone from the East Coast and Naples," he says. "The value is here."

Not every property seems like a value play—Schemmel currently represents a $38.45 million 11-bedroom, 17,200-square-foot estate on Longboat Key—but that price tag would double or triple in Naples or Palm Beach.

The threat of erosion, storms, and climate change isn't stopping the wealthy from plunking down millions on properties mere feet from the water.

"Any time I'd think there would be an exodus from those barrier islands," he says. "I'd be proven wrong."

#5615. The Latest Shift in How Appraisals Are Handled Could Save Homebuyers Hundreds in Closing Costs—Eventually

It’s typically the last hurdle for homebuyers—and the process is about to get a face-lift.

Last week, the Uniform Appraisal Dataset (UAD) 3.6, a major update to property valuation standards introduced by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, became mandatory for all new UCDP appraisal report submissions.

UAD 3.6 is a new, digital form that appraisers will use to evaluate homes. Now, rather than the appraiser meticulously jotting down notes in longform paragraphs, the new system will allow appraisers to use extensive drop-down menus and checkboxes to make their evaluations.

A proper appraisal can determine not only whether a buyer can qualify for a loan, but also whether they can save significant money at closing.

After a buyer makes an offer, their mortgage lender will order an independent appraisal to confirm the home is worth at least what's being borrowed against it.

If the appraised value comes in at or above the purchase price, the process moves forward as planned. But if it comes in low, that gap has to be resolved before the loan can close.

The logic behind the UAD 3.6 update, according to Fannie and Freddie, is to create a “data-driven, dynamic reporting structure to capture property and market information.”

This new form includes significantly more data fields, helping lenders and buyers better understand the property’s characteristics.

But with more detail comes a longer commitment.

“Be prepared for a lot more questions from the appraiser during the inspection,” explains Michael Mignogna, president of the Appraisal Institute.

“There’s a lot more data to include, so be prepared to answer questions about renovations, repairs, new systems like heating and air conditioning, appliances, etc., or have that information ready if no one with that type of information can be at the inspection.”

To that end, with UAD 3.6, appraisers will now not only grade individual rooms, but they can also highlight upgrades and features that might’ve been lost in the old system. So, features of a newly remodeled kitchen or new bathroom flooring get specifically noted, which will aid in the ease of deciding the home’s value.

Still, Mignogna is skeptical that this will have much of an impact on the final value.

“Not as much information is always known about the comparables, so expectations about condition/quality adjustments to the comps on a room-by-room basis should be tempered,” he adds.

The buyer almost always pays for the appraisal. The cost is typically a few hundred dollars, and it’s often rolled into closing costs. This is the case even though the appraiser is hired by the lender, not the buyer.

The hope is that because this new appraisal process is a clean, digital checklist, banks can review and approve it much faster, reducing delays.

For example, under the former process, lenders had the option to kick back the report for corrections if anything about the report was unclear, which could happen if the appraiser’s report didn’t cover every facet necessary.

When that happens, buyers may find themselves having to pay for expensive mortgage rate-lock extensions to keep their rates while they wait for the appraisal to clear.

Extension fees typically range from 0.125% to 0.250% (or up to 0.500% or more) of the buyer's total loan balance per extension period, often broken into 15-day increments.

On a $450,000 mortgage, a 15-day extension would usually cost between $500 and $1,000.

Given that closing costs already run a buyer anywhere from 2% to 5% of the total loan amount, or about $8,000 to $20,000 for a $400,000 loan, according to Bankrate, another couple hundred to a thousand dollars is nothing to scoff at.

But as the saying goes, all good things come with time, and right now, this new digital infrastructure may actually be coming at a cost to buyers as it finds its footing.

Clear Capital, a real estate valuation technology company, reported via National Mortgage Professional an average $65 increase in appraisal fees in markets where it has enough production volume to compare UAD 3.6 with the older UAD 2.6 format.

Additionally, Michael Farrell, president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, said that the number of field appraisers equipped to do UAD 3.6 is so limited at this point, demand bottlenecks are driving up prices for modernized reports. While older appraisals are being priced at around $550, modernized reports may cost borrowers closer to $850.

“It’s basically all roads lead to chaos,” Farrell explained to Scotsman Guide.

“From an originator standpoint, it's a delay. Delays cost money. Delays cost the consumer money.”

Mignogna, meanwhile, says it’s important to remember that fees are affected by far more than just the process.

“Appraisal fees are very specific to markets and are affected by the number of appraisers in a market, the demand for appraisals in that market, interest rates, and a host of other factors,” he says.

Having said that, the transition to the UAD 3.6 format continues to be slow and Mignogna concedes that lenders may bid up prices for the few field appraisers who are fully onboarded like in any “supply-demand situation.”

But while delays are happening as appraisers go through a “transition mode,” Mignogna says this won’t affect buyers' need for expensive mortgage rate-lock extensions.

“This is really only meaningful or significant in times of interest rate uncertainty or expected rate increases,” he says.

“The overall UAD 3.6 process is longer right now for the reasons above, but as the learning curve flattens, turnaround times will improve. It remains to be seen if the increased data requirements offset by UAD 3.6 familiarity gets us to the turnaround times seen before UAD 3.6 or faster turn times.”

With that in mind, it’s a good idea to ask your loan officer upfront if their specific appraisal management company has fully integrated the new digital system into their team.

While the UAD 3.6 mandate took effect on Nov. 2, 2026,  lenders may continue to submit revisions for existing UAD 2.6 reports through May 19, 2027.

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. #5614. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5613. The ‘Blue Wave’ Swept Top Homebuilding States. What Happens Next?

On Tuesday, the governor’s offices in five states were swept up by the “blue wave,” as Democrats were elected to succeed current Republican leadership.

Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas all flipped the governor’s seat from Republican to Democrat, after Democrats campaigned heavily on issues of affordability.

Of those five states, four rank in the top 15 on the Realtor.com® state Affordability & Homebuilding Report Cards for 2026, after making strides to expand housing supply under GOP leadership.

The report cards rank states on a points scale based on two major factors: affordability, such as the share of the state’s median income required to afford its median-priced home, and homebuilding, whether states are producing enough new housing to keep up with demand.

With affordability sticking out among the most important voter issues this year, how the new Democratic administrations improve, or at least maintain, states’ housing markets will be vital to whether they’re deemed successful.

Democrat Rob Sand was selected by the voters of Iowa in an 11-point victory over Republican Zach Lahn. He will  take over the position from outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Iowa was ranked second in the 2026 state report cards, earning a total score of 75.8 out of 100 for a grade of A. However, Iowa’s strength lies in the affordability aspect of the grading scale, not homebuilding.

The state’s median listing price sits at $282,886, which calls for just 25.4% of the $75,991 median income, giving it a Realtor Affordability Score of 0.96.

The downside comes in its homebuilding numbers. Iowa accounts for just 0.94% of the country’s issued building permits. While that number is on par with population—Iowa accounts for a 0.95% share of the country’s population—the state’s 56% new-construction premium indicates that builders are focused on larger, more expensive homes, rather than entry-level inventory and affordable builds.

In his “Truer Better Agenda,” Sand acknowledged that Iowa needs to build 21,000 more homes by 2030 to address the state’s housing shortage and improve affordability. Within his platform, he states his intention to work with the Legislature to ensure more homes, and more types of homes, are built.

“We need to cut the bureaucratic red tape that often stands in the way of that by simplifying the permitting and inspections process to reduce administrative time, redundant inspections, and costs for Iowa families,” reads Sand’s agenda.

Beyond building, Sand’s platform includes protecting renters from price gouging and removing interest from Iowa’s down payment and homebuyer assistance programs.

Jay Iverson, executive officer at the Home Builders Association of Iowa, said they have already been meeting with Sand to work on improving the regulatory process in the state, but the newly elected governor will face his share of challenges.

“He’ll still have a Republican-led House and Senate, so they’re going to have to figure out a way to get along. We fight the regulatory issues all the time, code updates, and all of the things that add significant costs,” Iverson told Realtor.com. “So we’re meeting with him even currently, before he’s sworn in, and hoping to deliver on that message of regulatory relief.”

Iverson said he’s looking forward to seeing Sand’s administration work with other governmental bodies to make improvements for Iowans, especially as the two parties come together.

“It’s just going to be a different environment. He sold himself during the campaign on, 'We should all be able to get along, let’s figure this out,’ and I think we’re going to hold him to that,” said Iverson. “I’m looking forward to that part, just seeing what actually happens and how it works. It’s never easy.”

Texas saw a major upset on Tuesday, when the state elected a Democratic governor for the first time since 1991.

Gina Hinojosa, who will make history as Texas’ first Latina elected governor, denied incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott a fourth term with her 7-point victory.

Texas is a consistent front-runner in the Realtor.com state report cards, coming in at No. 4 in 2026. The Lone Star State received a score of 71 out of 100 for a grade of A-.

Its success in the rankings is due to Texas being the nation’s largest homebuilder, accounting for 14.6% of all building permits issued in the country. This far outpaces any other state and is well above the state’s 9.3% population share.

The new-construction premium in Texas is only 7.6%, indicating that builders are adding affordable and competitively priced homes to the state’s inventory.

However, the state struggles slightly with affordability, with the median listing price of $364,749 taking up 32.5% of the state’s median income, giving it a Realtor Affordability Score of 0.66.

Housing has long been a priority of Hinojosa, who has been fighting against multinational corporations and predatory landlords since she was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2017. In 2025, she authored a bill that would prevent institutional investors from snapping up more than 10 single-family homes.

As governor, she intends to keep fighting corporate investors and price gouging that keep affordable housing and homeownership out of reach of Texans, according to her campaign.

The Texas Association of Builders feels positive about Hinojosa’s incoming administration and continued bipartisan efforts toward housing affordability in the state.

“She served on the Land and Resource Management Committee in the House this session and was very involved in a lot of the housing discussions and legislation on density, the need for more housing, and increasing housing supply, and was supportive of a number of these efforts during session,” TAB CEO Scott Norman told Realtor.com. “She was campaigning on some of these affordability issues on housing, so we’re excited to work with her and her new team.”

Norman also noted that the Texas Legislature has shown bipartisan efforts to rebuild its skilled workforce and expand training programs on every level, from public schools to trade schools and higher-education institutions.

“To get more people into these jobs that are AI-proof and that are lifetime careers that people can make a great living and own their own business, that’s something that has been very bipartisan,” said Norman.

This week, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms made history when she was elected Georgia’s first Black governor and the nation’s first-ever Black female governor.

The former Atlanta mayor captured 54% of the vote against her GOP opponent, Rick Jackson, and will take over from term-limited Republican Brian Kemp.

In the state Affordability & Homebuilding Report Card from 2026, Georgia ranked No. 12, receiving a B for its score of 63 out of 100.

Georgia’s affordability comes in far behind Iowa, with its considerably higher median listing price of $392,112 and slightly lower median income of $75,118. The state comes in with a Realtor Affordability Score of 0.68.

It’s homebuilding, however, is far more significant. Georgia accounts for 4.2% of the country’s building permits, behind only Texas, Florida, California, and North Carolina. The share of permits outpaces Georgia’s share of the nation’s population, which is 3.31%.

During her time as Atlanta mayor, Bottoms raised more than $700 million and helped build or preserve more than 7,000 affordable housing units, according to her campaign. She also introduced the City of Atlanta Housing Affordability Action Plan, which included a road map for increasing housing inventory.

As governor, she plans to create a Georgia Housing Fast Track initiative to further streamline permitting and establish an affordable housing trust fund to assist in the development of housing. Additionally, her platform includes expanding down payment and renter assistance programs throughout the state.

Democrat Amy Acton is the first woman to be elected governor of Ohio, beating Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 8 points. She will replace term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.

Ohio earned the No. 15 spot on the 2026 state affordability report card. It received a C+ for its score of 59.4 out of 100.

The state comes in with a healthy Realtor Affordability Score of 0.88, on par with the leading state of Indiana’s 0.89. Its median listing price of $277,348 is reasonable compared to its median income of $70,196.

Of all building permits in the U.S., Ohio accounts for 2.32% of them, slightly behind its share of the nation’s population, which is 3.48%.

The real issue for affordability in Ohio is the 84.6% premium on newly constructed homes compared to existing homes, which indicates that builders are catering to a more expensive market, rather than adding affordable homes to the state’s inventory.

Like the candidates above, Acton’s housing platform centers on removing red tape and streamlining the permitting process to make both new building and the renovation of older properties easier. She also plans to expand the Welcome Home Ohio program, created by DeWine, which provides grants and tax cuts for rehabbing older homes. She wants an expansion to encourage more new construction as well.

Placing restrictions on private equity firms and corporations buying up homes and providing support for first-time buyers are also among Acton’s housing plan, according to Columbus Underground.

The outlier on this list is Nevada. While the rest of the states rank in the top 15 states for affordability on the state report cards, Nevada comes in at No. 34 with a grade of C- for its score of 45.8 points out of 100.

Nevada accounts for 1.3% of the country’s total permits, slightly above its population share of 0.96%. Newly constructed homes come with an 18.5% premium compared to existing homes, which is not outlandish for this list.

The real struggle for Nevada is affordability. The state’s median income is $74,855, on par with No. 2 Iowa, but its median listing prices tower above at $491,936 for a Realtor Affordability Score of just 0.52.

Democrat Aaron D. Ford, the incoming governor, has his work cut out for him in the homebuilding sector.

The former Nevada attorney general held an 8-point victory over Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo on Tuesday  to become the state’s first Black governor.

Ford has laid out a number of pathways through which he intends to make housing more affordable to Nevada residents. Removing red tape and delays in permitting, developing vacant and underused land in the Las Vegas Valley, and expanding support for first-time buyers are among his top priorities.

Ford has also expressed that he will push back on recent tariffs imposed by the Trump administration that have made homes more expensive to build and purchase.

“Nevada families are being forced to absorb higher costs caused by tariffs on essentials like aluminum, steel, lumber, and even basic fixtures like bathroom vanities,” said Ford in this “Affordable Nevada” plan. “A $1,000 increase in the price of a new home pushes an estimated 115,000 households out of reach of homeownership—a price spike working families cannot afford.”

Allaire Conte contributed to this report.
