Citing the original beadboard walls and boxy door frames, Miller could immediately picture the property’s origin story.

“You hear about somebody building a house with their bare hands, and this is the type of house I think about, you know?” he says. “The old-school North Carolina farmer gets done for the day and he’s like, adding onto his house, or he’s just doing cool stuff because that’s what he needs to survive and live on the land. That’s the vibe I get from this house.”

Known as “Old House Adam,” Miller has been transforming historic North Carolina homes for 15 years. While he says his team can “save anything,” he’s careful with choosing projects that are also good business, avoiding properties that would be “financially irresponsible” to tackle.

“If we’re not able to make the numbers work, sometimes we have to pass on really cool, beautiful projects,” he explains.

The Chester House was a particularly exciting case for Miller and his team—which includes his wife, Jessica Miller, a talented interior designer and portrait artist.

“We actually beat out a developer that was hunting the property,” he shares, noting that this plot of land was exceptionally desirable, given its access to a 48-acre nature preserve. “It was really pretty awesome.”

They were also able to secure the two properties on either side of the Chester House, where they’ll erect “heirloom farmhouses,” leveraging vintage floor plans and salvaged materials to create something new with an old-school feel.

Although the home ended up needing much more work than initially anticipated, Miller was able to restore its original character while adding a few modern luxuries.

Two gorgeous and generously sized bathrooms were added—even if they both required extensive changes to the footprint of the home.

The kitchen underwent a more extensive renovation than he typically carries out in these kinds of projects, receiving fully-customized cabinetry. And the home’s most defining features—like the original wood floors—were given their moment to shine.

“You don’t want a house where you’ve pulled all the character out of it, but you also don’t want a house that feels like it’s still 1886,” he says.

For Miller, that means finding a balance between keeping original features and making additions that “embrace the imperfections of the house.”

In an “awkward” corner, they added “interesting bookshelves” to give the space new purpose. Built-ins and storage space were added to make the home more functional. And aesthetics were chosen to provide a mix of on-trend features and classic design, which Miller points out, are sometimes one in the same.

Miller also believes that it’s important to choose the right materials when breathing new life into an historic property.

“You’ve got to pull in a little bit of personality,” he says. “People don’t acknowledge this. It’s the material choices. If you stick to old-school materials and there’s no real plastics involved or synthetics, then you can get a lot more look for the money.”

Speaking of quality, Miller, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, is also careful to make sure his projects tick all of the boxes needed to qualify for a potential buyer to use a VA loan. He says that understanding the “code and qualifications” of a VA loan is important for renovators and builders, “Because then everybody gets to qualify and participate in home ownership.”

“I talk to a lot of veterans, and they’re like, ‘You can’t get a loan on an old house,’ and that’s 100% not true,” says Miller. “You can’t get a loan on a bad old house. But a good old house? There’s a lot of them. There’s a lot of these old houses that have survived, and they hit all the notes.”

Miller couldn’t have used a VA loan to acquire the Chester House for renovation, joking that it was in such disrepair that “VA wouldn’t have even sent somebody out to look at it originally.” But he says the loan option is a great tool, and even used one for his own home, which was built in 1906.

Now that the Chester House has been given a second chance, “even though it’s as old as it is, it would be a perfect home for a VA loan,” Miller explains.

“We replaced all the siding, there’s no chipping paint. All the windows open and operate correctly. The grading was all professionally done, so there’s no intrusion of water in the basement,” he says. “It’s got a new roof on it, the foundation doesn’t have any cracks greater than an eighth of an inch… so if you can ensure a house has all the qualifications, then you can renovate an old house and veterans can still get loans on them.”

Beyond going the extra mile to ensure a dwelling can be a great home for anyone, Miller loves to see what a renovation can do for a community.

“So many people drive by it. They’ve watched it just fall apart,” he says. “And everyone’s like, ‘Man, I wish somebody would save that thing,’ and that’s cool, too. To be the guy that people associate with watching a house fall down and all of a sudden you get to watch it be built back up.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. #5589. Court Report: Tuccori Settlements on Hold as Judge Requests Further Logistics

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

Tuccori settlement on hold after judge request

The approval of settlement agreements with more than 20 real estate companies in a major antitrust lawsuit filed by recent homebuyers challenging commission practices in the residential real estate market has been put on hold by a judge following a request for more information.

The settlements in the Tuccori v. At World Properties commission lawsuit were preliminarily approved back in May, but final approval has been put on hold as Judge Lindsay C. Jenkins has put in a request for additional information on five topics.

Firstly, Jenkins asked for clarification on a concern that was previously raised at a hearing: The valuation of claims filed, namely that “resolving 1/8 of all claims for 1/8 of what you paid to resolve the other 7/8 of all claims does not imply you valued the 1/8 and 7/8 equally on a per claim basis.”

Other requests include how each settler’s “ability to pay and transaction volume influenced their proposed settlement,” further information for the court to be able to arrive at the “net expected value of continued litigation,” benchmarks for “substantive adequacy from other indirect purchaser class actions,” and lastly, an estimation of per claimant and per class member recovery.

The National Association of Realtors®, one of the settlers in the case, said in a statement that it “continues to believe the Tuccori settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the class.”

“The settlement offers meaningful protections across the industry, providing a broad release for REALTOR® members, REALTOR® associations, MLSs, and those brokerages that meet the settlement’s eligibility requirements,” the statement read. “NAR remains committed to fostering fair, transparent, and pro-consumer real estate markets while providing resources and value to our REALTOR® members nationwide.”

NAR added that the judge’s request is “a routine part of the class action settlement approval process, consistent with the judge’s role in evaluating the fairness of the settlement.”

“NAR is committed to abiding by the judge’s request to provide the Court with information in a timely and efficient manner, including working with the other parties, to demonstrate the settlement is fair and reasonable,” the statement concluded.

Briefs on the topics are due by Dec. 14, after which time the court will say if it needs further responses.

Fair housing lawsuit against Bank of America dismissed

A racial-discrimination lawsuit filed against Bank of America and a Virginia-based appraiser has been dismissed.

The suit was filed by Darchelle Braxton, a Black woman who last summer attempted to secure a loan for home improvements on an investment property. She claimed in her filing that an initial appraisal ordered by Bank of America valued her property at $135,000, but a subsequent second appraisal valued it more than 50% higher, at $208,000.

The appraiser—Velox Valuations—filed a motion to dismiss, refuting Braxton’s claims that it provided a “shockingly low” valuation on her property due to alleged “material errors, omissions, and inconsistencies,” which stemmed from racial bias. Such errors included allegedly using an incorrect map reference, using an incorrect neighborhood valuation, only using two comparable properties, inconsistent descriptions of the property’s condition, and more.

The suit was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

With the many legal battles the portal has faced as of late, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business” during its Q3 2026 earnings call.

CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann added that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

The portal is currently still facing a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5588. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5587. Century Communities Promotes Jim Francescon to President

As part of its long-term succession planning process, Century Communities has promoted Jim Francescon to president, effective January 1, 2027. Francescon currently serves as executive vice president, corporate operations.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” says Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success, and growth.”

Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman and Rob Francescon, who currently serves as CEO and president, will solely serve as CEO. As president, Jim will oversee the company’s home building operations, land, and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth.

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest home builders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” says Rob. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Before serving as executive vice president, Jim was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and prior to that served as corporate vice president. Jim also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation, and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

“I am honored to take on this role and grateful to our board, Dale, and Rob for their confidence,” adds Jim. “We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of “A Home for Every Dream.””

#5586. Minnesota Remodeler Is Banned for Life After Demolishing Rooms and Skipping Out

A Minnesota contractor promised homeowners he could transform their properties with extensive renovations. Instead, many say they were left with unfinished work, empty bank accounts and little to show for the tens of thousands of dollars they had handed over.

Now, Ryan David Pietron, and his company, Affordable Home Remodeling, LLC., have been permanently banned from Minnesota's residential construction industry and ordered to pay more than $1 million after a state investigation found they had defrauded dozens of homeowners out of a combined $518,000, according to the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.

"Pietron would perform token demolition work, or none at all, before disappearing with his customers’ money," the AG's office said in a statement.

On Nov. 5, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announced a judgment against Pietron and the company, requiring them to pay $518,000 in restitution to victims, another $518,000 in civil penalties to the state and $33,000 to cover the attorney general's costs and legal fees.

“Pietron played fast and loose with people’s home renovation dreams and needs,” Ellison said. “He counted on people giving up and moving on. Instead, Minnesotans reported this scheme to my office, and now he’s permanently out of this business and will pay for his fraud.”

In a separate criminal case brought by Wright County Attorney’s Office, Pietron pleaded guilty on Nov. 3 to felony theft in connection with some of the same conduct that was the subject of the AG’s civil investigation.

The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office sued Pietron and Affordable Home Remodeling in October 2025 on behalf of Minnesota homeowners who were left with unfinished renovations and losses totaling thousands of dollars.

Pietron was never licensed as a residential building contractor and was banned by the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry from claiming to be a licensed contractor—but told customers he was licensed anyway, according to the attorney general’s office.

In an attempt to squeeze more money out of homeowners, investigators say Pietron issued fake progress updates and forged phony invoices.

In one case, a homeowner had hired Pietron to complete work on her kitchen in October of 2024. Nearly a year later, the homeowner was out of town and contacted Pietron to find out the status of the work.

Pietron told her that a crew was currently working on the home. But when the homeowner checked the home’s security cameras, they discovered no one had arrived at the property.

Pietron gave other excuses for the delay including that several trucks had broken down. He then disappeared from the job completely and took the homeowner’s money with him, according to the complaint.

In another case, a customer who had hired Affordable Home Remodeling waited several months for work to begin on his home, only to be given an invoice for supplies which had allegedly been ordered on the homeowner’s behalf.

But when the homeowner contacted the supplier listed on the invoice, they had no record of such items having been ordered by Affordable Home Remodeling. Pietron allegedly made off with $30,000 for work on that property that had never started.

Some of the homeowners managed to track him down and when they did, he had promised to issue them refunds but failed to do so.

Investigators identified more than 50 Minnesota homeowners who lost a combined $518,000.

The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office is urging homeowners to research contractors and companies before signing agreements, request important information in writing and carefully review contracts and other documents.

While hiring a licensed contractor does not guarantee a successful home improvement project, there are many protections for consumers who hire licensed contractors.

Licensed contractors are required to carry liability insurance and property damage insurance. Consumers can also use a free license lookup tool maintained by the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry to verify whether a contractor is properly licensed.

Eligible consumers who obtain a judgment against a licensed contractor for fraudulent or dishonest conduct can recover up to $75,000 from the Contractor Recovery Fund if they are unable to collect the judgment from the contractor.

#5585. EXCLUSIVE: Former NFL Star Chris Simms Sells 300-Year-Old Greenwich Home For $5.5 Million

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has sold his historic Connecticut estate for $5.5 million—after reducing the initial $8 million asking price several times.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately led to Simms landing a buyer for the dwelling, Realtor.com® can exclusively reveal. The property has closed for $5.5 million.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor plan that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now moving to a new state and want to pass their current dwelling to a new owner who will treasure it as much as they have.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

Simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the New England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

#5584. Humanoid robot maker Agility Robotics debuts on the Nasdaq after SPAC merger

Agility Robotics Inc. debuted on the Nasdaq today after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company.

SPAC deals provide a simpler path to public markets than a traditional listing. In such transactions, a shell company floats its shares and then merges with a privately held business. That business effectively takes the SPAC’s place on the stock exchange where it’s listed.

Agility merged with an investment vehicle called Churchill Capital Corp XI Corp. on Wednesday. The deal and certain “related financings” together pulled in $465 million, a sum that excludes transaction fees. Agility will use the capital to bring its latest Digit 5 robot to market and add manufacturing capacity.

Digit 5 (pictured) is a nearly six-foot-tall humanoid robot with a 20-hour battery life. It moves using custom actuators based on so-called cycloidal drive technology. That’s a motor design that trades off some speed for increased lifting power: Agility says that the Digit 5 can carry up to 50 pounds at a time.

The robot’s batteries are made by a British startup called Nyobolt Ltd. They use niobium, a metal most commonly found in superconductors and jewelry, to speed up charging. Agility says that the Digit 5 can be recharged in just nine minutes, a fraction of the time required by earlier technologies.

The robot runs some of its software on Nvidia’s IGX Thor system-on-chip series. The most advanced chip in the lineup, the T7000, combines a 14-core central processing unit with a computer vision accelerator and two graphics processing units. One is an embedded GPU with 2,560 cores while the other is a standalone chip originally designed for workstations.

Digit 5 also makes use of Nvidia’s HALOS software toolkit. The suite includes algorithms that help robots avoid hazards. Additionally, HALOS provides resources that make it easier to secure the safety certifications required for commercial deployment.

Agility says that it has received more than $300 million worth of pre-orders for Digit 5. Its customers include Toyota Motor Co. and GXO Logistics Inc., a publicly traded transportation company. Agility claims that it also has three other large customers in the manufacturing sector along with a pipeline of more than 30 prospects.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Agility Chief Executive Officer Peggy Johnson. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.”

Agility plans to make Digit 5 available through an early access program in the first half of 2027. General availability is slated for later that year. The company will manufacture Digit 5 at a  70,000-square-foot factory in Salem, Oregon with planned capacity of up to 10,000 robots per year.

#5583. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

#5582. Olivia Culpo Brings 5-Week-Old Son to His First 49ers Game—Inside the Guest Room She Turned Into His Nursery

Olivia Culpo brought her 5-week-old son, Roman, to his first San Francisco 49ers game to cheer on dad Christian McCaffrey—months after transforming her guest room into his nursery.

The model, 34, took to Instagram to share a glimpse at the family game day, which saw her, Roman, and her daughter, Colette, 1, stepping out to watch McCaffrey, 30, take on the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium.

One of the snaps showed off their game-day attire, which included a 49ers shirt with "Daddy" on the back.

Another image showed Roman in his stroller and was captioned, "Roman's first game."

The beauty mogul also shared a photo of her and her daughter, which she captioned, “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom.”

Culpo also shared a video of her taking their children to embrace their dad after the game, adding, “We’re back with one more little fan in the stands this season. A little more love coming along for the game this season."

The model revealed that she welcomed their second baby on Sept. 29.

Months before, she revealed that she had transformed their guest room into a nursery. She shared that she overhauled the room her sister Aurora Culpo's kids Remi, 7, and Soleil, 5, tend to use when they visit.

"New baby's room for now. I wanted to keep the twin beds because Remi and Solei sleep here when they come over," she wrote alongside an image of the nursery she shared on her social media page in June.

The room boasted a neutral aesthetic with an animal theme.

At the time, she explained, "We also don’t know the baby’s gender yet, so this feels perfect neutral for now. Honestly, newborns don’t really sleep in their room in the beginning anyway because they’re eating around the clock. That’s one of the reasons I’ve never felt the need to find out the gender to 'have the nursery ready.'"

That same month Culpo revealed she and her spouse were in the process of giving their $14.5 million property a head-to-toe overhaul to ensure it was looking its very best by the time the newest member of their family was born.

Culpo and McCaffrey purchased the Fryman Canyon, CA, dwelling from actor George Clooney in 2025, but they are now steadily eradicating all traces of the "Ocean's Eleven" star from the home in a bid to turn it into their dream family abode.

Revealing a sneak peek at the changes, Culpo pointed to one particular area of irritation that she has since transformed: dual bathrooms that sat next to each other with their own doors.

"Remember the two bathrooms next to each other that made no sense? All gone! I moved the door to the kitchen and now it will be a scullery,” Culpo wrote alongside an image of her hallway with the offending bathrooms on full display.

But the model did not stop there, moving on to several other spaces in the house, all of which have been given a stunning facelift, outfitted with new wallpaper, paint, and upgraded floors.

She then shared before-and-after images of the dining room, revealing that the space has been completely cleared of all previous decor, including the industrial lighting fixture that hung in the middle of the room, as well as the orange curtains and white wood-paneled ceilings.

The space has, instead, been given a fresh new aesthetic, complete with patterned wallpaper, hardwood flooring, exposed wooden beams, and an elegant crystal chandelier hanging at the center of the space.

“Currently … Dining table and chairs going in soon!," Culpo captioned the video of the newly revamped room.

The dwelling serves as the primary residence for the model and her husband, who is currently one of the leading players on the San Francisco 49ers.

The opulent six-bedroom, six-bathroom abode sprawls across 7,354 square feet, giving the couple plenty of room for their growing family.

Inside, the home boasts a library, screen room, and wine wall.

Culpo and McCaffrey purchased the home from Clooney, 65, who bought it from Fleetwood Mac singer Stevie Nicks for $2.2 million in 1995.

One month after splashing out a staggering sum on the property, Culpo gushed about it on Instagram.

"Now onto my next project, the most exciting one of all. Our forever home. So much original character to protect in this home, it’s going to be such a special project," she said.

The couple's purchase came four months after they tied the knot in a lavish Rhode Island ceremony attended by their close friends and family.

At the time, Culpo told People magazine, "I loved every part of my wedding. I love my husband and the people we got to celebrate that day with."

Three months before they said "I do," Culpo revealed she was ready to start expanding her family, joking that she was going to "rip out [her] IUD” and “start trying immediately” after the wedding.

The former Miss Universe also holds the keys to a $3.5 million property in Encino, CA, which she purchased in 2019 and which served as her and McCaffrey's main residence during the NFL offseason.

In 2021, she told Architectural Digest she purchased the five-bedroom, seven-bathroom property to get away from the "noise" of Hollywood.

“I realized I really wanted something that felt more calming, like a sanctuary almost. A respite from the city,” she said at the time.

McCaffrey previously owned a North Carolina mansion, which he sold in 2024 for $12.5 million, and a Charlotte, NC, condo, which he let go of in 2024 for $3 million.

In recent months, Culpo has confessed that the couple keep their romance alive during her spouse's busy season by "prioritizing date nights at least twice a month."

“During the season, it can be a little more difficult. Just prioritizing one-on-one time," she told E! News in September.

#5581. Atlassian shares fall 17% as slower subscription growth forecast overshadows earnings beat

Shares in Atlassian Corp. fell more than 17% in after-hours trading today on a forecast for slower subscription growth from the Australian collaboration software company.

Its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results beat analyst estimates. The stock had nearly doubled between Atlassian’s August report and late October.

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, Atlassian reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.65, up from $1.04 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $1.772 billion, up 24% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.43 per share on revenue of $1.71 billion.

Most of the growth came from cloud, where revenue rose 31%, to $1.302 billion. Customers kept adding Jira and Confluence seats in the quarter, according to the shareholder letter, including in business teams well outside software development.

Growth in Data Center, the self-managed product line Atlassian will retire in March 2029, slowed to about 5%, leaving revenue there at $391 million. The company said those customers are expanding less as they plan their moves to the cloud.

Subscription annual recurring revenue came in at $6.812 billion at the end of September, up 22.5%. Remaining performance obligations jumped 44%, to $4.746 billion. Enterprise customers are behind that increase, according to the company, with deals getting larger and stretching over several years.

Atlassian made money on an unadjusted basis for the second quarter running, with net income of $91 million, or 35 cents per share. Chief Financial Officer James Chuong put that down to keeping costs in check while revenue grew. Free cash flow climbed to $463 million on strong collections, and Atlassian returned $581 million to shareholders through buybacks.

On the product side, more than 87% of enterprise cloud customers now use Rovo, the company’s artificial intelligence assistant. Upgrades to the Teamwork Collection bundle rose sevenfold from a year ago to more than 3,000 customers. Annual recurring revenue from the larger Service Collection bundle is now above $1 billion, spread across more than 70,000 customers.

Chief Executive Mike Cannon-Brookes used the earnings release to argue that enterprise AI has reached “an inflection point.” Model power alone no longer sets anyone apart, he said. Platforms that give people and AI agents shared context to work from will pull ahead by his account, and Atlassian has “never been better positioned” to be one of them.

For the second quarter, Atlassian expects revenue of $1.825 billion to $1.835 billion, a little ahead of the $1.82 billion analysts had forecast, with cloud revenue growth of about 27%.

Most of Atlassian’s fiscal 2027 targets edged higher in the update. The company now sees full-year revenue growth of about 13.75%, three-quarters of a point above its August forecast. Because customers pulled Data Center purchases into fiscal 2026 after the retirement announcement, this year’s revenue comparisons are tougher.

Total revenue growth should pick up again in fiscal 2028, Atlassian said. Investors sold the stock on a different number. The company expects subscription annual recurring revenue growth to slow to about 18.5% by fiscal year-end, down from the 22.5% it just reported.

#5580. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5579. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, an Astra model built to keep vulnerability research in scope

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for authorized vulnerability research.

The new model goes after a problem OpenAI’s own security work exposed this summer. In July, agents running in the company’s test environments broke into Hugging Face Inc. while pursuing an assigned task. GPT-6 Cyber was trained to stay inside the targets a researcher has authorized, and the safety test OpenAI built for the launch draws on that incident.

That test, ExploitGym Honeypot, gives the model a difficult assignment and surrounds it with supporting services that are deliberately easy to compromise. Attacking any of those services counts as a scope violation.

With no deployment safety instructions in place, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds in 0.07% of graded runs. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6-Cyber, did so 5.51% of the time. Adding the instructions brought GPT-6 Cyber’s observed rate to zero.

OpenAI rates the new model at Critical, the top cybersecurity tier in its Preparedness Framework and the same classification Astra received at its September launch. GPT-5.6-Cyber had been rated High. The company says GPT-6 Cyber beats Astra on most cyber tasks, and an early research campaign on Firefox turned up 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla Corp. rated high severity. Mozilla has since shipped fixes for many of them.

Irregular, an AI security lab named in the system card, put the gap with Astra closer, finding the two broadly comparable apart from stronger GPT-6 Cyber results on long multistep tasks. Neither model got past fully hardened targets in OpenAI’s own challenge set.

GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cyber-specific model OpenAI has released this year. Like the first, GPT-5.4-Cyber, it sits behind an application process. Initial access is limited to a select group of approved customers in Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak program meant for offensive-style work such as penetration testing and red teaming. Those customers reach the model through the company’s application programming interface and Codex, and API requests have to come from approved networks by default.

Google LLC also put vetted defenders first when it launched Gemini 4 Argon in September. A week later Anthropic PBC rebuilt its Cyber Verification Program around three access tiers.

OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber will reach all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and GPT-5.6-Cyber is now opening to every customer in the tier. Critical infrastructure defenders get a Daybreak Red group of their own. On the defensive side, the company is extending early Astra access through Daybreak Blue to more organizations and to individual security researchers.

#5578. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5577. Why Now Is the Time to Prepare Senior Homes for the Spring Market

For seniors preparing to sell a home they’ve lived in for decades, fall may be the ideal time to start downsizing before spring brings a new wave of buyers. When the weather starts to cool and the leaves start to fall from the trees, it can feel like a natural time to reset, to refresh a living space and prepare for the next life chapter.

As families shift holiday decorations, reorganize storage and prepare for the end of the year, it can also be a natural opportunity to begin sorting through a lifetime of furniture, keepsakes and belongings before a home goes on the market.

Nan Hayes, VP of Business Development at Caring Transitions, a company specializing in transforming the way seniors and their families transition through life’s stages, talks about the various aspects of preparing now for homeselling later.

Why is fall a good time to begin downsizing before a spring sale?

Fall can be a good time to adjust old habits and set new goals. As the season changes, it creates a natural opportunity to take stock of our homes and begin letting go of things we no longer need.

For homeowners considering a spring home sale, fall is a good time to begin downsizing and decluttering. Starting months before listing provides time to address repairs, sort through belongings and make decisions without the added pressure of an active home sale. As a bonus, a more organized home can also make holiday entertaining easier.

Homeowners can choose to sort, donate, sell, gift or dispose of excess belongings themselves, or bring in professionals to handle some of the more time-consuming tasks. Either way, starting early can help ensure the home is ready when it is time to list.

For real estate agents, the journey from lead to listing can take several months. Timelines become longer when homeowners are waiting for more favorable market conditions, completing home preparations or waiting on another life event, such as end of the school year, or the birth of a child.

For older adults who are downsizing into a senior living community or other care setting, the process may take even longer. Selling a family home in later life can be a major task. Many times, the home holds a lot of memories as well as a lot of ‘stuff.’ Beginning early gives families time to plan the transition and make thoughtful decisions along the way.

How can decades of belongings affect a home’s perceived space?

Even a spacious home can feel smaller when closets, cabinets, garages and rooms are filled with belongings.

Reducing excess items before listing helps buyers focus on the home rather than its contents. With fewer distractions, buyers can better understand the storage space, room sizes and possibilities the property offers.

Removing excess belongings and highly personal items can also help buyers imagine themselves living in the home. The space feels more open, and the features of the property become easier to see.

Why can waiting until a home is listed create unnecessary delays?

Once a home is listed, the clock starts ticking. If the home is not yet market-ready, the remaining tasks make the home less appealing than others on the market, and can interfere with showings, or complicate the sale and closing process.

Rushing through all the tasks at the very end isn’t a good solution either. If sorting, organizing, packing, donating, selling belongings, repairing the home, and moving all have to happen at once, the home seller can quickly become overwhelmed, and they may stop the entire process.

Starting early separates the emotional work of downsizing from the time-sensitive work of selling.

How can agents approach emotionally difficult downsizing conversations?

When clients are overwhelmed by years of possessions, unsure where to begin, or suffering from decision fatigue, they need a clear plan and calm communication that stems from a place of empathy rather than urgency.

Instead of saying: “You really need to get rid of all this!” Try: “You don’t have to figure this out all at once. Let’s start with what you would like to take with you, and then we’ll come up with a plan for everything else.”

This shifts the conversation away from what the client feels they have to give up or get rid of, so they can instead focus on what comes next. For many homeowners, belongings represent decades of memories, family milestones, and important moments. Recognizing that emotional connection can make difficult conversations easier and help clients feel supported rather than rushed.

Agents do not have to solve every part of the transition themselves. They can provide direction, connect clients with reliable relocation resources, and help break a large project into manageable steps.

How can families use the holidays to start sorting, organizing, and letting go?

The holidays may provide a natural opportunity to start on home projects because families are already spending time together. Rather than turning every family gathering into a major downsizing event, use the time to share memories, make a few decisions, and start conversations about the future.

Families might look through photographs, collections or keepsakes together. Consider digitizing large collections so they can be shared with family members. Share the stories behind meaningful belongings or write those stories down.

Invite children and grandchildren to choose items that are meaningful to them. Tackle one closet, cabinet, collection, or small area together. Identify which belongings might be donated, gifted, sold, or included in an estate sale or online auction.

Contact professional downsizing, relocation, estate sale, and auction resources early to request estimates and reserve time before spring schedules begin to fill. The goal is not to spend the holidays cleaning out the house or emptying every room. It is simply to start a conversation, make a plan, complete a few manageable tasks that can help build momentum. In short, a little progress now can mean fewer decisions and less pressure when it is time to list the home.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5575. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5574. David Muir Shares Rare Look at Personal Life Ahead of His Birthday—Inside His $7 Million Lakeside Estate in Upstate New York

When it comes to his personal life, famed journalist David Muir tends to keep quiet, but the “World News Tonight” anchor recently pulled back the curtain just before his 53rd birthday.

In a Nov. 7 Instagram post, the ABC News anchor shared a wholesome update—a snap of his German short-haired pointer, Axel, as the pair set out to enjoy the fall foliage.

Although Muir let the photo speak for itself—offering nothing more than an autumnal leaf emoji as the caption—he occasionally uploads content of Axel, usually to show off their outdoor adventures.

In a 2025 interview with People magazine, the broadcaster shared some rare insight into his home life, noting that while he’s based in Manhattan for work, he enjoys retreating to a spot just outside his hometown of Syracuse.

“I’d say my most comfortable element is being outside, covered in mud,” he told the publication, adding that he had recently taken a trip to his property in upstate New York, enjoying the surroundings despite the fact that it had been “pouring rain.”

In 2019, Muir purchased a $7 million property on Skaneateles Lake—a small town about a 30-minute drive from Syracuse.

“This job takes me all over the world, and I can’t think of a better place to catch my breath,” he told Syracuse.com at the time.

The 4,300-square-foot abode is a single-family home set on a 6-acre plot of land with water access. The six-bedroom, 2.5-bathroom dwelling was built in 1890 and seems to be the perfect place to escape from the bustle of the city—or a job as demanding as Muir’s.

“When you’re out there on the lake, smelling the same air that you smelled when you were on your BMX bike back when you were a kid, there’s something really fueling about that and connected about it,” he told People magazine in 2025. “You just feel like you’re home again.”

Over the years, Muir has invited his Instagram followers to enjoy the dazzling lake views he enjoys during his weekends away.

In a 2020 post, he remarked, “I love being home,” in a caption of a photo of himself cracking a smile while enjoying a boat ride across the lake.

A few distinct features of Muir’s historic home have taken up real estate on his Instagram profile, as well, including the charming wraparound porch that hugs the Skaneateles Lake property, which made an appearance in a 2022 post he shared for his sister’s birthday, where he made a note to give a shoutout to “porches.”

He purchased the 2,280-square-foot abode for $4.2 million in 2013, the same year he became the host of “World News Tonight,” following in Diane Sawyer’s footsteps.

Located on West Fourth Street, the three-bedroom, three-bathroom structure was built in 1877 by Alexander M. McKean, and Muir put it on the market for $7.5 million in April 2025.

“Inside, the original details of this 15 foot wide house have been lovingly restored,” the listing explained. “The renovation maintains and respects the character of this remarkable home, while bringing it completely up-to-date, upgrading electricity, plumbing, and gas service but keeping and restoring original details including hardware, flooring, fixtures, and historic plaster medallions and moldings throughout.”

Perhaps the most stunning feature of the townhouse was the primary bedroom, which spanned the entire fourth level of the building. With a bed area that faced over quiet gardens and a full wall of closets, the suite also included a spacious office and a windowed bathroom with a vintage claw-foot tub.

The home lingered on the market for a few weeks before it was removed and relisted, but nearly six months later, it was sold for $6.85 million.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5573. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5571. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.
