#5541. AI cyber resilience and the trust gap

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante and Krista Case

Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets.

In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake?

Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit.

Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes.

Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments.

We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions:

These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require.

Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI.

Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested.

These findings come from a small sample of in-depth interviews conducted with our partner Qualitate. The conversations allowed us to explore what customers have tested, the additional security work their own AI creates and what it takes to resume a business process safely. One healthcare practitioner phrased the disconnect between confidence and readiness as follows:

No, we have not completed any tabletop exercises as it pertains to an AI agent or other similar attacks. We’re highly confident because these are scenarios similar to non-AI incidents we have handled before.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Across the interviews, respondents who did express confidence often drew heavily on existing ransomware and incident response playbooks. Their experience with non-AI incidents understandably provides a degree of trust. But it also raises a concern in that organizations may assume that an agent taking an incorrect action can be handled in the same way as an insider or external attacker doing something similar. We don’t believe existing playbooks cover all scenarios.

Rather, we believe that assumption needs to be tested against the specific demands of an agent incident. The interviews revealed a mixed picture of true validation:

Complete business recovery requires an organization to reconstruct a sequence of authorized actions, identify incorrect outcomes, repair downstream effects and safely resume the affected business process. Demonstrating that the full sequence works is a nontrivial exercise.

The speed, scale and interconnected nature of agent activity makes that even more challenging. Actions can affect multiple systems and processes, creating consequences that existing playbooks need to account for. We see a risk of false confidence when organizations assume that their experience with traditional non-AI incidents will translate automatically. Testing needs to establish how well their capabilities hold up under the conditions an agent can create, which may be novel.

Bottom line: Evidence of validated, end-to-end business recovery from an agent incident remains limited in our study. We believe organizations should exercise their existing playbooks against realistic agent scenarios, with safe business resumption as the measure of success.

Our interviews raised questions about tooling, maturity and the processes needed to prove that existing capabilities work for agentic AI. Two findings as shown below highlight the limited reach of detection and reconstruction capabilities in the organizations studied:

One healthcare practitioner’s assessment of the controls already implemented underscores the trust gap:

No, for the ones that have been implemented, we have not tested or validated that they work.

— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech

Enterprises already have identity systems, application logs, data protection tools and the like, along with established incident response processes. They are trying to extend these capabilities to AI. The central challenge is validating that the tools can reconstruct activity across an entire agent workflow.

Agents interact with multiple applications, invoke tools and autonomously trigger downstream actions. Each system may capture its own events without providing a coherent record of the complete workflow. Incident response requires correlating those records to establish which agent acted and under what authority, then tracing the tools it invoked and the changes that resulted.

This reminds us of the early days of disaster recovery, when organizations would test failover but hesitate to test failback because they were nervous about what might happen. We see a similar reluctance to ask questions that could expose gaps in readiness or cause downstream problems. The concern is whether the connected tools and processes will hold up under realistic agent incident conditions.

Bottom line: Organizations need to exercise the full agent workflow under realistic conditions, including a plausible worst-case event, and validate that their tools and processes can reconstruct the activity and support the response.

Our assessment of the field interviews highlights both the technical and business dimensions involved in a recovery. An AI agent can use legitimate access to change a record incorrectly or send a message that should never have been sent. A backup may work and the restored systems may appear healthy while the business remains unable to resume safely.

StorageTek veteran Fred Moore, an early mentor to Dave Vellante, coined the phrase: “Backup is one thing, recovery is everything.” The scope of recovery continues to expand as organizations consider the consequences of agents acting across business systems.

A director of information security at a media and entertainment firm described the problem this way:

We could restore our systems, we could restore within our recovery objectives, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that it’s safe. The bottleneck here would be trust.

— Director of information security, media and entertainment

Recovery point objectives or RPO and recovery time objectives or RTO are the so-called business metrics. But business users need more meaningful key performance indicators that resonate — specifically, what a trusted, viable service looks like and how that condition can be verified. That includes establishing who needs to participate in recovery and who signs off that operations can safely resume.

This direction needs to come from the top down; and be verified bottom up. Business leaders must define the requirements, with IT and security acting as partners to provide the underlying technology and help achieve the required outcome. The responsibility extends beyond the traditional data protection team’s work of recovering data and systems.

Incorrect transactions, human error and failures that ripple across systems have existed for a long time. Agentic AI adds two complications:

That requires a comprehensive view of what went wrong and what needs to happen to recover. The organization must be able to trace the agent’s activity and evaluate the resulting business state against clear criteria for safe operation.

Bottom line: Recovery requires explicit criteria for verifying that a business service can be trusted and clear responsibility for approving its return to operation. The business must set that direction, with IT and security providing the capabilities to carry it out.

Humans in the loop help organizations restrict what agents can do. Resilience also has to account for what happens when a human misses an incorrect action or cannot keep pace with agents operating at machine speed. Two statements from the same CIO illustrates the issue:

So the given scenario will be detected by human beings before the AI agents can take the actions.

If it really happens, currently we do not have the capability to roll back the agent’s action.

— Chief information officer, real estate and construction

The first statement shows confidence that human oversight will catch the problem. The second acknowledges a missing “undo command” if the human oversight fails. This captures why approvals and recovery testing need to advance together. Reliance on human intervention can bring a false sense of security and defer attention to the recovery details needed when a mistake gets through.

Our field study also revealed how customers are weighing the tradeoffs around autonomy, with organizations generally still containing what their agents can do. Those decisions become particularly important when agents receive authority to take remedial actions during an incident or recovery.

The level of autonomy granted should reflect the risk of the action. Before allowing an agent to approve or execute a remedial action, organizations need to understand the consequences of an incorrect decision. That calls for a tiered approach built around two considerations:

We expect human approval to become an increasingly significant bottleneck over the next six to 12 months. Organizations need to establish these boundaries as they begin trusting agents to take more remedial actions.

Bottom line: Human oversight and recovery testing need to develop together. As organizations delegate more authority to agents, they must account for mistakes, the limits of human review and the risk associated with each action.

A retail practitioner described a viable approach to rehearsing an agent incident and we see this as a best practice. Specifically, this firm replays the agent’s actions in a replica environment, investigating the root cause and using granular snapshots to understand the transactional effects. The respondent explicitly confirmed that the approach had been tested in the sandbox with the following statement:

Yes, if the agent went across multiple systems, my approach is to replay this within my sandbox environment, which is a full replica of all of the systems.

— Director of information technology, retail

The value of this approach is in reproducing the sequence of events and investigating their effects across systems. Our assessment of what such an exercise should confirm is anchored on three outcomes:

We see these as minimum viable expectations for the evidence an exercise should produce.

We use the term digital twin here as a broad analogy for this approach. A fuller digital twin would involve a richer representation of business processes, dependencies and state. We believe the industry still has work to do in that direction, and that work will become more important as enterprises use AI to run critical functions. In addition, it will further expand the notion of recovery as the state of the business will become increasingly more complicated as agents perform more of the work.

The respondent also acknowledged a limitation saying: larger transaction volumes could require more time for reconciliation. Replaying actions and identifying affected transactions provides useful information, while the time needed to resolve their consequences remains an open item. Richer simulations of business environments could help organizations test agent behavior and prepare for what a failure might look like in production.

In other words, testing the recovery sequence in a variety of scenarios inside a digital twin of the business prior to pushing the process into production. Further, this “red teaming” exercise must be ongoing – expanding the concept of continuous data protection into the state of a firm’s operations in more granular snapshots.

Bottom line: This example offers a practical approach to reproducing agent actions, investigating their consequences and rehearsing recovery. Its value also points toward the need for richer representations of the business processes those agents affect.

If a chief information security officer takes one action from this study, we recommend exercising an agent incident affecting one consequential workflow already in production. Choose a workflow in which an agent has permission to act across multiple systems, and design the exercise to include incorrect actions taken with valid credentials and permissions.

The exercise should also include a scenario requiring human approval. This helps establish the boundaries around where autonomy is appropriate and where human oversight remains necessary.

Validation by the business owner is essential. Security teams can establish that an incident has been contained and provide evidence of what happened. The business owner must determine whether the resulting business state is acceptable. That decision needs to account for the consequences of the agent’s actions and any remediation work still required.

The exercise should document what was proved, what remains untested and which teams are responsible for closing the remaining gaps. That evidence should also inform decisions about how much authority an agent receives. The organization needs to understand its ability to reverse or correct actions and recover their consequences as it considers granting greater autonomy.

The discussions at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit reinforced the themes emerging from the field study. Conversations with vendors, practitioners and researchers underscored the need to build resilience and recovery into agent deployments from the outset. Evidence that these capabilities work becomes essential as agentic workloads move into production.

The challenge includes preserving and recovering a trusted business state when an agent produces an incorrect outcome despite having legitimate credentials. Organizations need to understand how those outcomes affect their operations and what it will take to address them.

Existing investments in data protection infrastructure, security and recovery remain critical. The work ahead is to identify the gaps that emerge under the new requirements and pressures created by enterprise AI. That requires collaboration across internal teams and with vendors to understand where capabilities need to improve.

Bottom line: We believe trust in enterprise AI requires tested evidence that organizations can understand what agents have done, stop them, reconstruct their actions and recover to a healthy business state. Our research indicates that organizations still have work to do to demonstrate that their existing security and recovery capabilities can meet that requirement.

#5540. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5539. Real Estate Expert Matt Nuzie Explains Buying and Selling a Home at the Same Time

The article explains how homeowners can plan their finances, decide whether to buy or sell first, and coordinate closing dates when moving from one home to the next.

TRUMBULL, Conn., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --

How can homeowners manage buying and selling a home at the same time? A HelloNation article provides the answer, featuring insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert with REMAX Right Choice in Trumbull, Connecticut. The newly published article explains how financial planning, mortgage options, and closing dates affect both sides of the move.

The article explains that selling your current home first gives homeowners certainty. Once the sale closes, they know exactly what they have for a down payment and a price range.

Selling first also removes the risk of carrying two homes. The trade-off is that homeowners may need temporary housing, storage, or two moves.

Buying a new home first lets homeowners move on their own schedule. The article notes that it can mean covering two mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance, and utilities, so a conversation with a lender should come before any offer.

How Do Mortgage Options Affect Buying and Selling?

According to the article, mortgage options often decide the order. Some buyers need the equity from their current home for a down payment, while others qualify for financing that lets them buy before selling.

Matt Nuzie recommends reviewing income, savings, and the current mortgage with a lender before touring homes.  A home sale contingency makes a purchase dependent on selling the buyer's current home. It offers protection, but many sellers prefer offers without one when they have several to choose from.

Matt Nuzie notes that scheduling both closings close together lets homeowners move directly from one home to the next.

Closings can be delayed for ordinary reasons, such as a lender's request for documents or an inspection issue, so building in some breathing room is wise.

A rent-back agreement can let sellers stay in the home for an agreed period after closing. Short-term temporary housing is another option when the dates don't line up.

How Can Homeowners Prepare for Unexpected Costs?

The article recommends starting early on cleaning, small repairs, and listing photos, since they often take longer than expected.

Moving, storage, repairs, and temporary housing can add up quickly, so setting aside extra savings helps.

Matt Nuzie also emphasizes keeping the real estate agent, lender, and attorney informed of deadlines, and reading contract terms closely before signing.

How to Buy and Sell a Home at the Same Time features insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert of Trumbull, Connecticut, in HelloNation.

Is It Better to Buy or Sell a Home First?

According to Matt Nuzie, it depends on your finances, your moving plans, and the local real estate market. Selling first brings financial certainty, while buying first offers more flexibility with the move.

Matt Nuzie explains through insights featured in the article that a home sale contingency makes a purchase dependent on selling an existing home. It offers protection, though many sellers prefer offers without one.

Can You Close on Two Homes at the Same Time?

The article explains that homeowners can schedule both closings close together. Financing or inspection delays can still shift the timing, so some cushion is wise.

What Happens if Closing Dates Do Not Match?

Based on insights from Matt Nuzie, Real Estate Expert of Trumbull, Connecticut, homeowners may consider a rent-back agreement or short-term temporary housing. Both can provide extra time between transactions.

Matt Nuzie is a REALTORÂ® with REMAX Right Choice, 105 Technology Drive, Trumbull, CT 06611. Each Office Independently Owned and Operated.

#5538. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to having extramarital affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia Corp. said on Sunday it’s launching an “independent investigation” into reports that its founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence plot, shortly after he admitted he “had been intimate” with a Singapore-based executive whom U.S. officials accuse of spying for China.

In response to the allegations, the Republican-led foreign affairs and intelligence committee of the U.S. Congress has asked Huang (pictured, right) to testify this week at a closed-door briefing on the chipmaker’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.” The request came after the New York Times reported last month that the CEO had been targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.

The accused spy is a woman called Alice Huang or Huang Le (left), of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. Alice Huang is the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed. It had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s high-end graphics processing units to China, prompting U.S. officials to begin monitoring her. Those officials have apparently determined that Alice Huang is an asset of the Chinese intelligence services, tasked with passing commercial secrets back to Beijing.

In a statement earlier today, Nvidia’s board of directors said that though it has no reason to believe that either U.S. national security or the company’s secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the statement said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The company added that Huang supports the investigation into what happened and has vowed to cooperate fully.

A report by Axios earlier today cited a draft email written by Huang to company employees, in which he admitted to having an illicit romantic relationship with Alice Huang and took full responsibility for his actions. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

U.S. intelligence chiefs will be concerned because Nvidia’s powerful chips sit at the center of the artificial intelligence boom and give America a critical advantage over its geopolitical rivals. The company’s dominance of AI computing means that Huang is one of the most influential people in the industry, and he has forged close ties with the Trump administration.

The alleged spy reportedly tried to take advantage of Huang’s close links to America’s policymakers. Not only was she tasked with learning more about the company’s secrets, but also persuading Huang to lobby for the company to be allowed to ship its most advanced processors to China.

It’s not clear how much influence she was able to exert on Huang, but last year he successfully petitioned the Trump administration to allow more GPUs to be exported to China. He later struck a deal to sell limited numbers of the company’s second-most powerful chips to China.

So far, nothing has been said of Huang potentially losing his job or being removed from the company, but Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives told Gizmodo that such an outcome is possible. “This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” the analyst said.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research cautioned that it has not yet been proven that Alice Huang really is working for China’s intelligence agencies, but said even if it isn’t, it’s going to become a major distraction for Nvidia. “It won’t help anyone, except possibly Nvidia’s competitors,” he said. “This is going to be a big test for the chipmaker, but it and Huang will be hoping they can brush it aside until it only becomes a footnote in the AI industry highlights of 2026. We’ll see.”

The investigation follows a rough week for technology firms on Wall Street, which have weathered a selloff that began earlier this month and gained traction after a series of disappointing earnings results in recent days. So far this month, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index has lost almost $1 trillion in value.

Nvidia’s stock has fallen 21% over the last month and is now basically flat in the year to date. Its market capitalization sits at just over $4.5 trillion, down from its peak of just over $5.7 trillion in October.

#5537. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5535. Bitcoin ETF Outflows Hit $430M as Hong Kong Expands Its BTC Market

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin ETF outflows reached $430.2 million at the end of Thursday, as institutional investors continued withdrawing capital from US-listed spot products. Meanwhile, Hong Kong is expanding its crypto investment market, with four spot Bitcoin ETFs now available to investors.

Hong Kong’s private banking and wealth management assets reached HK$12.9 trillion ($1.65 trillion) in 2025, marking a 24% annual increase. Net fund inflows also climbed 79%, according to the latest Hong Kong Private Wealth Management Report 2026.

The contrasting developments put Hong Kong’s growing digital asset industry in focus. While American investors reduce exposure through listed products, Asian financial institutions are building new ways to access Bitcoin.

US spot Bitcoin ETF products recorded $430.2 million in net outflows on November 5. Fidelity’s FBTC led withdrawals with $199.9 million, followed by BlackRock’s IBIT at $105 million. Grayscale’s GBTC recorded another $49.9 million in withdrawals, while Franklin Templeton’s EZBC lost $32.9 million.

The latest session pushed November’s cumulative Bitcoin ETFs outflows to $869.8 million across four trading sessions. Net withdrawals across the latest seven finalized sessions reached approximately $1.36 billion.

That pressure follows a brief recovery on November 4, when the funds attracted $74.6 million. However, the latest withdrawals suggest institutional demand remains fragile.

The selling also comes as Bitcoin struggles to regain momentum. Investors are now watching if continued redemptions translate into further pressure on the underlying market.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Hong Kong already operates a dedicated Bitcoin ETF market, rather than simply preparing to introduce cryptocurrency investment products.

The city has four spot Bitcoin ETFs listed on its exchange:

Hong Kong also offers two futures-based products: the CSOP Bitcoin Futures ETF and Samsung Bitcoin Futures Active ETF.

The first three spot products launched on April 30, 2024, making Hong Kong an early Asian market for regulated Bitcoin investment products. MicroBit subsequently joined the market in August 2025.

However, Hong Kong’s Bitcoin ETF market is not immune to withdrawals. November month-to-date flow figures from a regional ETF tracker showed outflows of $5.71 million from ChinaAMC, $1.58 million from Bosera HashKey and $68,880 from Harvest.

These figures show that institutional appetite remains uneven across both markets. Hong Kong’s smaller ETF market has not yet demonstrated that it can absorb the selling pressure seen in the United States.

Nevertheless, the wider financial industry continues building its digital asset exposure.

According to the Hong Kong Private Wealth Management Report 2026, 43% of surveyed firms have added cryptocurrency ETFs or exchange-traded products to their offerings. Another 25% are developing digital asset trading platforms, custody services or product ranges, and a further 28% plan to invest in digital assets within the next two to three years.

Hong Kong’s wider asset management industry reached HK$42.2 trillion, according to the Securities and Futures Commission. This gives traditional financial institutions a substantial pool of capital from which to develop new investment products.

The longer-term opportunity extends beyond immediate Bitcoin ETF subscriptions. Hong Kong is developing an institutional ecosystem that includes regulated products, custody services, and established wealth management firms.

The latest US withdrawals show that institutional demand can reverse quickly. However, Hong Kong’s expanding infrastructure displays that the competition for digital asset capital across global financial centers is far from over.

#5533. Google advances agentic AI custom silicon expanding TPU family with 8tx and 8i Max

Google LLC today introduced two new specialized silicon chips for artificial intelligence to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit architecture family, aimed at higher compute density and secure inference.

At Google Cloud Next 2026 in April, Google introduced two specialized TPUs in the same generation, 8t for large-scale training and 8i designed for real-time reasoning. At the time, the company said it released the chips to handle demanding AI workloads across two primary tasks: building the models and running them.

Today’s expansion includes two new specialized chips across additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest possible compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx designed for secure and confidential inference.

Google said TPU 8i Max aims to scale compute and memory, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the high-bandwidth memory of TPU 8i. This gives processors as much memory as possible to handle data without swapping it out.

Additionally, the company added that 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the same rack footprint, lowering the floor space it takes per square foot and per watt in data centers.

This allows the new eighth-generation TPUs to provide customers with a purpose-built accelerator for larger models and the industry’s current push toward ultra-large context windows.

A context window acts as an AI model’s working space: how much data it can consider while answering a question. A larger window lets it work across a longer document, conversation history, audio file, video or collection of code. But expanding it comes at a cost. Processing and repeatedly consulting more information puts greater demands on chips to swap data in and out, requiring more on-chip memory and stronger connections that move data between processors.

Adding more on-chip memory reduces the need to move data between processors, lowering latency and reducing the power an AI model needs to “think” about information.

Google said it developed 8i Max alongside pushing massive context windows for its Gemini frontier model, which supports the 1 million-token industry standard. That represents roughly 750,000 words or 1,500 pages of text. Although flagship models tackle 1 million tokens, smaller models often support narrower window sizes between 128,000 and 256,000 tokens.

Google said it optimized TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference, designing the chip for regulated enterprises and governments that want to run frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside the most sensitive data.

Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but when an AI model processes that same information, it must be decoded. Built on the same architecture as the TPU 8t, with custom AMD central processing unit hosts, the 8tx builds in a secure enclave directly into the hardware layer that keeps sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated.

The company said the architecture pairs training-grade compute with fast inference, meaning organizations can run and customize models on a single confidential system. The combination allows regulated services and industries to fine-tune models using private data, distill large models into smaller ones and train agents through reinforcement learning.

All of this can be done without migrating data between separate clusters, which could expose sensitive information to leaks.

#5531. Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending Launch Federal Credit Lab Platform

Federal Credit Lab provides publicly available data visualizations and analysis on the allocation of federal credit across the U.S. economy.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending launched the Federal Credit Lab, a publicly available data and insights platform providing data and analysis of the U.S. government credit portfolio to generate actionable insights for policymakers, program administrators, researchers, and the public.

The United States government is one of the largest lenders in the world. Its portfolio contains over $5 trillion in cumulative outstanding loans and loan guarantees. In Fiscal Year 2026 alone, Congress authorized nearly $1 trillion in new loan and loan guarantees spanning over 100 programs and 20 federal agencies.

Federal Credit Lab is a joint initiative of two nonprofit organizations, the Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending, aimed at making this portfolio data more readily accessible to inform better program assessment, delivery, budgeting, and design.

"Federal credit is one of the most powerful and least understood sets of tools by which policymakers can mobilize private capital to address national challenges," said Jack Moriarty, Executive Director of Lafayette Square Institute. "Our objective in building Federal Credit Lab with our partners at the Center for USA Lending is to enhance our collective understanding of this toolkit to inform the next generation of industrial policy and the allocation of capital to the people and places that need it."

"Modern systems and better information lead to better policy. The Federal Credit Lab puts that premise into practice. It is a platform that makes the government's lending enterprise substantially more visible, accessible, and accountable. We see this as a foundation, one we hope to build on in partnership with federal credit agencies," said Doug Criscitello, Executive Director of the Center for USA Lending.

"By applying analytics to the complex workflows across the federal credit portfolio, Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending are creating conditions for government and capital markets to better serve workers and communities in every zip code," said Damien Dwin, Founder and CEO of Lafayette Square and Board member of Lafayette Square Institute.

"The Federal Credit Lab platform aspires to make the world of federal credit accessible to a much wider audience of stakeholders by centralizing and unifying a previously disparate set of data sources," said Laura Hohenberger, Senior Associate for Data Analytics and Policy at Lafayette Square Institute.

The launch of the Federal Credit Lab featured a joint event in Washington, D.C. that included a platform demo and expert speakers. Additional programming on select thematic areas in the federal credit portfolio is slated throughout 2027. Lafayette Square Institute and the Center for USA Lending invite public feedback on applied research questions for future analysis.

About Lafayette Square Institute Lafayette Square Institute (LSI) is a nonprofit policy and data analytics platform committed to aligning private capital with the public interest. Through deep bipartisan relationships, innovative finance tools, and data analysis, LSI mobilizes investment in the people and places that need it.

About Center for USA Lending The Center for USA Lending is a nonpartisan organization advancing a modern, effective credit ecosystem. It connects public and private stakeholders, elevates borrower needs, and promotes the use of modern technology to ensure access to capital for the borrowers federal credit is intended to serve.

#5530. Exclusive: FormAssembly overhauls its platform to expand into AI-powered process automation

FormAssembly Inc., a provider of online data collection and workflow automation software, today announced a complete platform overhaul that expands its capabilities beyond building forms to automating complex business processes using artificial intelligence.

The new platform, which the company said took seven months to develop, combines form creation, workflow automation, integrations and compliance management in a single no-code environment.

It also introduces conversational AI agents that can collect information through natural language interactions and support for the Model Context Protocol, enabling external AI agents to interact with FormAssembly’s software.

The launch marks a significant expansion for the 20-year-old company, which has traditionally focused on helping organizations collect structured information securely and integrate it into business applications. “We’re about how people share information with organizations and what happens after that,” said founder and Chief Executive Cedric Savarese.

The new platform builds on the AI assistant FormAssembly introduced last October, which enabled users to generate forms and configure workflows using natural language instructions. The latest release extends those capabilities to entire business processes, including approvals, document generation, electronic signatures and payments.

For example, a municipal government could describe an application process for obtaining a permit to hold an event in a public park. The platform’s assistant, called Fai, could then generate the necessary forms, approval workflows and documentation requirements.

“You can explain what you need in plain English to your agent, and the agent will build the entire process in a couple of minutes,” Savarese said.

FormAssembly claims the AI-assisted builder can reduce development time from days or weeks to minutes. Savarese said the company based those estimates on recreating existing customer workflows using the new platform.

A second major addition is conversational intake agents that replace traditional forms with interactive voice or text conversations. The agents use predefined data structures to guide conversations, answer questions and convert unstructured responses into information suitable for downstream systems.

The agents can also personalize interactions using previously collected information, although Savarese emphasized that access to that information is restricted by default.

FormAssembly uses frontier AI models, primarily from Anthropic PBC, rather than developing its own. Savarese said the company has zero-retention agreements with Anthropic and OpenAI Group PBC to protect customer information.

The revamped platform also adds governance capabilities that evaluate workflows against predefined compliance policies before publication. Organizations can use built-in rules or define their own requirements based on internal policies and applicable regulations. Potential violations are flagged for human review rather than automatically blocked.

MCP support and application programming interfaces enable customers to create and manage FormAssembly workflows through external systems without accessing the software’s traditional interface.

Savarese said this approach could protect established software companies from the risk that AI agents will make conventional software-as-a-service applications obsolete.

“People will use AI agents, but they use AI agents to drive software, not to replace it,” he said.

The company isn’t positioning itself as a comprehensive competitor to business process management vendors such as ServiceNow Inc. Instead, it intends to concentrate on processes that begin with collecting information from people.

Existing customers won’t be forced to migrate immediately. Savarese said migrations aren’t planned until January, and pricing for existing customers remains uncertain. More sophisticated automation capabilities could carry additional charges depending on customers’ current subscriptions.

FormAssembly, founded in 2006, raised its first outside funding of $10 million in 2019 after 13 years of bootstrapping. The company says it has thousands of customers, particularly in regulated industries such as healthcare, financial services, education and government.

#5528. Dorsata, Inc. Notifies Patients of Metabase Data Security Incident

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dorsata, Inc. has become aware of a data security incident involving the Metabase third-party software it uses that may have involved the protected health information belonging to patients. Dorsata is sending letters to potentially involved individuals to notify them about this incident and provide resources to assist them.

On or about August 12, 2026, Dorsata received a notice that the Metabase business intelligence software it uses contained a security vulnerability. They immediately patched the software and began an investigation with the assistance of independent cybersecurity experts. The investigation determined the Metabase security vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to its database platform that stores medical information related to patients of Dorsata's healthcare provider partners between August 10, 2026 and August 12, 2026. Dorsata then reviewed the data involved in the incident to identify the individuals whose information may have been involved. Please note that there is no evidence of the misuse, or attempted misuse, of any potentially impacted information.

On October 21, 2026, Dorsata began sending notification letters to the individuals potentially involved in this incident providing them information about what happened and steps they can take to protect their information.

Based on the investigation of the incident, the following personal and protected health information may have been involved in the incident: name, address, patient ID, date of birth, vitals data, treatment information, treatment location, provider name, vaccines, medications, health insurance information, and patients' medical history contained in a patient's medical records. Social security numbers, driver's license number, and financial information were not involved.

Dorsata takes the security of patient information very seriously and has taken steps to prevent a similar event from occurring in the future, including installing the security patches and updates Metabase has provided to entities who use their software. The notification letters Dorsata sent to potentially affected individuals also include information about steps that individuals can take to protect their information.

Dorsata has established a toll-free call center to answer questions about the incident and related concerns. The toll free phone number is 800-655-5832 and is available from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm ET, Monday through Friday, excluding major holidays.

#5526. NAR membership proves more resilient than expected, topping 1.46 million

NAR told directors membership totaled 1,469,127 at the end of September, 22% above budget and 1.5% below a year earlier. Dues revenue was about $220 million of more than $250 million, while expenses ran about $7 million under budget.  AI Summary

It is no secret that the National Association of Realtors (NAR) had a challenging few years. From facing a sexual harassment scandal, navigating the commission lawsuits and the implementation of the resulting settlement, to looking to create a more accountable and responsible version of the trade group, NAR has experienced its fair share of growing pains. But, when it comes to the association’s financials, 2026 was far better than anticipated.

In an update at NAR’s 2026 NXT Board of Directors meeting by NAR’s 2026 Treasurer Craig Sanford, it was revealed that at the end of September, the association had 1,469,127 members, 22% better than the 1.2 million members the association had budgeted for and just 1.5% lower than membership a year ago. In addition, Sanford said membership renewals for 2027 are tracking in line with where they were in 2026.

Revenue from membership dues accounted for roughly $220 million of the more than $250 million in revenue NAR had reported as of the end of September. Sanford also noted that NAR’s expenses as of late September had come in roughly $7 million better than budgeted, but that he expected some of those savings to be diminished by fourth quarter advocacy spending due to the recent midterm elections. Despite this, Sanford said that NAR’s cash and investments remain strong, allowing the trade group to meet its upcoming settlement payments while still investing in new products and services for its members.

“In my two years as treasurer, I have seen the start of one of the greatest financial modernization in transformation in NAR’s history,” Sanford said. “We have implemented a new accounting system along with accounting and budgeting tools, moved to monthly accrual accounting, selected and onboarded the new auditor, managed through massive personnel changes, implemented zero-based budgeting and now we are minutes away from voting to send our third consecutive balanced budget to the Board for approval.”

Despite this progress, Sanford said that the work is not done, instead it’s just getting started.

The next stage of this work kicked off with the approval of three budgetary members by the board of directors. Sanford noted that this budget was created after stringent review of each department, resulting in a budget “that is more intentional, more strategically aligned and better positioned to support [NAR’s] core mission while maintaining financial discipline.”

During the meeting, the board overwhelmingly approved a 2027 operating and advocacy budget of $280,169,801 in gross revenue, and $246,952,390 in gross expenses. Over 90% of the directors also approved a 2027 consumer advertising campaign budget of $12 million in gross revenue and $13.696 million in program expenses. Additionally, over 95% of the directors approved a recommendation that found that the capital expenditure needs identified for 2027 technology total $2.42 million and that the capital expenditure needs identified for 2027 building needs total $3.06 million.

In addition to approving budgetary measures, the board also voted on proposed amendments to the bylaws of the institutes, societies and councils. During the meeting, Brown noted that the amendments were reviewed by NAR’s general counsel and were deemed to be “not inconsistent with the policies and constitution” of NAR.

The proposed amendments were approved by 864 directors voting in favor and six opposed.

Beyond voting on these measures, the meeting also saw the installation of the 2027 leadership team, including 2027 NAR President Christine Hansen, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, President-elect Colin Mullane, First Vice President Pete Kopf and Treasurer Patti Fitzgerald. The leaders were approved by the board of directors back in May at NAR’s Realtors Legislative Meetings.

#5524. AWS commits $100M in AI and cloud credits to health groups in underserved communities

Amazon Web Services Inc. today committed $100 million worth of artificial intelligence and cloud technology over five years to health organizations working in underserved communities around the world, provided to recipients as AWS credits.

The new AWS Health Impact Initiative is taking aim at a cost problem that AWS says is keeping many of those organizations out of the current wave of AI adoption. AWS points to survey data to explain the focus on credits.

An independent survey of 83 of the more than 400 organizations supported under the company’s earlier AWS Health Equity Initiative found that 60% saw cost as the main barrier to cloud adoption where they operate. Most ranked AWS credits as their highest-priority need. That program began in 2021 with $40 million behind it, and the total had grown to $60 million by the time the last of it was handed out in July 2024.

Timing matters too. A World Economic Forum forecast cited by AWS has generative AI use climbing faster in health care than in any other field. If the organizations closest to underserved patients fall behind on adopting it, AWS argues, health gaps will widen.

Agents and AI are reshaping health services, said Dr. Rowland Illing, chief medical officer and director of health care and life sciences at AWS, and they “too often don’t reach the communities that need them most.” Illing framed the initiative as an extension of the company’s stated aim of democratizing AI and cloud-based health technology.

Any area of health care is eligible, and AWS has singled out three for added weight. The first is access to health services, where AWS wants to support diagnostic testing and stronger health infrastructure in places such as rural areas and low- and middle-income countries.

A second area covers research into women’s and children’s health, with better data and more inclusive studies as the goal. Women’s health draws just 5% of health research funding, the company said, and as many as half the medicines given to children lack pediatric clinical validation.

Healthy food is the third area. AWS said malnutrition among pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and adolescent girls has climbed 25% since 2020 in the 12 countries hit hardest by the global food and nutrition crisis. Projects there could improve food distribution or predict food security patterns.

Recipients AWS highlighted include women’s health data nonprofit Eve’s Ark, which collects research datasets that are at risk of disappearing when a lab closes or a grant ends. Co-founder and Chief Executive Melissa Antal Iftimie said the group started with a small AWS award and “a single at-risk dataset.” The archive now holds more than a petabyte of women’s health data on AWS, and the group is building a secure research environment where scientists can work with it.

In Haiti, primary care provider Care 2 Communities runs a network of community clinics that has served 350,000 people and handles almost 120,000 patient visits a year. Its electronic medical records sit on AWS, which brings centralized, real-time data to clinics in rural parts of the country. School meals for more than 2.35 million children in India come out of kitchens run by the Akshaya Patra Foundation every school day, and the foundation uses AWS to run those kitchens and get meals out to schools.

Eligibility runs well past health charities to government agencies, research institutions and companies, and AWS will consider a project at any stage up to full production.

Organizations with an AWS account team can submit proposals through it, and a public portal is open to everyone else. Each application has to estimate how many lives the project will improve, and AWS goes through submissions every week. Successful applicants receive credits sized to their own AWS Pricing Calculator estimate of what a project needs, or a starting allocation of up to $10,000. Awardees have 12 months to use the credits and can ask to have that window stretched to 24.

#5523. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5522. loanDepot’s Q3 loss grows while it chases 2027 break-even

loanDepot reported a $29 million net loss in Q3 2026, larger than the prior quarter, as high mortgage rates weighed on originations. The lender is pivoting toward higher-margin products like home equity loans and purchase mortgages, which helped lift gain-on-sale margins even as volume fell sequentially.   AI Summary

loanDepot widened its net loss in the third quarter of 2026 as it sold mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), repurchased debt and leaned into higher-margin products.

The California-based nonbank lender reported a $29 million net loss in Q3, compared with a $7 million loss in the prior quarter, according to its earnings release Monday. Founder and CEO Anthony Hsieh told analysts that the quarter was challenged by unexpectedly higher interest rates but said the company remains focused on gaining market share despite depressed volumes.

“Getting over the seasonality of Q4 and Q1, and of course not knowing where the market will end up next year, but if it stays at this level, we are very confident that we’ll get to a break even of profitability by first half or mid next year,” Hsieh said.

loanDepot originated $7.05 billion in mortgages in the third quarter, down 12% from the prior quarter but up 7.8% year over year. Purchase loans made up more than 61% of total volume.

On a unit basis, originations rose 7% quarter over quarter, helped by the company’s expansion into home equity products. Management said loanDepot estimates it ranked among the top three nonbank home equity lenders in the third quarter based on volume, a shift that helped push gain-on-sale margin to 399 basis points, up 54 basis points from the second quarter.

“Since my return last year, we increased origination volume by 8%, grew unit volume by 33%, increased purchase volume by 10%, improved return on marketing by 14%, and reduced our cost to produce by 16%,” Hsieh said. “These results reflect the success of our ongoing efforts to diversify revenue sources, increase operating efficiency, and improve the scalability of our platform.”

The company now expects its productivity and efficiency initiatives to deliver $25 million in annualized cost savings through the remainder of 2026, more than double the previous estimate of $12 million.

loanDepot continued to shrink its balance sheet and reduce debt through MSR sales in the quarter. The company closed the sale of $10 billion in agency MSRs and agreed to sell an additional $9 billion in government MSRs, a transaction expected to close in October.

After these moves, loanDepot’s servicing portfolio stood at $115.7 billion at the end of the quarter. Proceeds were used to repurchase $87 million of senior notes at an average price of 88% of par.

Chief Financial Officer David Hayes said the combination of MSR sales and debt repurchases reduced net debt obligations by about $114 million, strengthened liquidity and improved financial flexibility.

Even with those steps, leverage remains elevated. Debt obligations, net to total equity, were 6.5x at the end of the quarter, up from 4.8x a year earlier. Hayes said the company is working “actively” to address nearing debt maturities and is pursuing financing options to refinance or extend with financing counterparties ahead of 2027 bond maturities. He did not provide more details during the calls with analysts.

Looking to the fourth quarter of 2026, loanDepot guided to origination volume between $4.5 billion and $6.5 billion, implying potentially lower production than Q3. However, it expects gain-on-sale margin between 315 basis points and 355 basis points.

Management framed the outlook as a continuation of the pivot toward more profitable products, a larger purchase footprint and a leaner cost base in the face of persistent rate pressure.

“While elevated interest rates remain a headwind for mortgage demand, we believe the actions we have taken to diversify our product offerings, expand our purchase market presence, improve efficiency, strengthen margins, and optimize our balance sheet have positioned loanDepot to emerge from this cycle as a stronger and more competitive company,” Hsieh said in a statement. “We remain focused on growing market share, improving profitability, and creating long-term value for our shareholders.”
