#5521. Automax.ai Wins Innovation Challenge at LendingTree's 2026 Lender Summit

Automax.ai is modernizing the appraisal process by improving the experience for homeowners, lenders, and appraisers.

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LendingTree, Inc. (NASDAQ: TREE), the nation's leading online financial services marketplace, hosted the annual LendingTree Mortgage Summit this week at the Knight Theatre in Charlotte, N.C. bringing together top lenders, industry experts and fintech innovators to assess market outlook, and the evolving mortgage industry. During the event, Automax.ai was named the winner of the 2026 LendingTree Innovation Challenge for its AI-powered platform designed to modernize the property appraisal process.

Nine fintech companies competed in this year's Innovation Challenge, each delivering a seven-minute pitch to a panel of industry judges and Summit attendees. Participants showcased innovative solutions aimed at improving the mortgage experience, increasing operational efficiencies, and addressing challenges facing lenders and borrowers. Automax.ai, an AI-native property appraisal platform, stood out for its approach to simplifying a traditionally time-consuming part of the mortgage process.

Presented by founder and CEO Humza Ahmed, Automax.ai demonstrated how its technology combines digital property inspections, 3D modeling and artificial intelligence to streamline the appraisal process from start to finish. Rather than relying exclusively on traditional, in-person inspections, the platform enables a certified data collector or homeowner to conduct a guided video walkthrough of a property, capturing more than 800 data points, including details about the condition and quality of flooring, ceilings and other property features.

The information is used to generate a detailed 3D model that appraisers can review and verify. Depending on loan eligibility and applicable requirements, the process may support an appraisal waiver or allow an appraiser to use Automax.ai's suite of AI-powered tools to complete the appraisal report.

The platform also provides lenders, underwriters and processors with greater visibility into the status of an appraisal throughout the process. Automax.ai's end-to-end approach delivers average appraisal turnaround times of one to three days, with reports completed within 24 hours following inspection. The company also reports savings of approximately $50 to $100 compared with traditional appraisals, offering the potential to reduce costs and delays in the homebuying process.

Innovation challenge participants were evaluated by judges and audience members across six criteria: increased conversion and originations, ability to implement, market relevance, product quality & UI/UX, and demo quality and salesmanship. The judges panel included Jessica Gardner, CMO of Armed Forces Bank and Academy Bank; Erin Dee, SVP, Chief Innovation Officer at BankSouth Mortgage; and Chad Smith, CEO of Envoy Mortgage.

"This year's Innovation Challenge demonstrated the creativity and entrepreneurial spirit driving the mortgage industry forward," said Will Adams, Head of Sales at LendingTree. "All nine participating companies presented compelling solutions to some of the challenges lenders face today. Automax.ai stood out for its practical approach to addressing a critical part of the mortgage process, with technology that has the potential to reduce costs, accelerate timelines, and improve the experience for lenders, borrowers and appraisers."

Through initiatives like the Innovation Challenge, LendingTree is connecting industry leaders with emerging innovators, spotlighting solutions that help lenders operate more efficiently while creating a simpler, more transparent experience for consumers. Automax.ai's recognition reflects the growing opportunity for AI-powered technology to address longstanding industry challenges and deliver meaningful improvements throughout the mortgage journey.

LendingTree, Inc. is the parent of LendingTree, LLC and several companies owned by LendingTree, LLC (collectively, "LendingTree" or the "Company").

LendingTree is one of the nation's largest, most experienced online financial platforms, created to give consumers the power to win financially.  LendingTree provides customers with access to the best offers on loans, credit cards, insurance and more through its network of approximately 770 financial partners.  Since its founding, LendingTree has helped millions of customers obtain financing, save money, and improve their financial and credit health in their personal journeys. With a portfolio of innovative products and tools and personalized financial recommendations, LendingTree helps customers achieve everyday financial wins.

LendingTree, Inc. is headquartered in Charlotte, NC. For more information, please visit www.lendingtree.com.

Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX have joined a growing list of companies rejecting OKXICE tokenized stocks trading platform, bringing the total objections to 67. The update added Palantir, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Meta to the list. That puts 56 of the 62 companies originally selected for the platform among those objecting to their shares being traded through the proposed venue.

OKX–ICE Stock Venue’s Issuer Objections Reach 62Boeing and ServiceNow have raised objections to the venture’s proposed symbols, leaving eight of the 63 originally proposed symbols without a disclosed opt-out.⚠️ Personal market analysis only. NFA — manage risk and DYOR.… pic.twitter.com/CXjQRpQOnH

The development comes as Musk recently attracted attention for responding to a separate ICE-backed Hyperliquid initiative. The billionaire replied “Interesting” to investor Stanley Druckenmiller’s October 29 announcement about investing in Trade[XYZ], which is partnering with ICE to bring Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures to US markets.

The growing opposition presents a significant obstacle for OKXICE tokenized stocks plan, a joint venture between cryptocurrency exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange.

The proposed platform aims to bring tokenised versions of US stocks onto blockchain infrastructure, allowing investors to trade around the clock using stablecoins such as USDC. But companies have increasingly exercised their right to prevent unaffiliated platforms from offering tokenised versions of their shares.

Tesla and SpaceX appeared in OKX-ICE’s November 2 notice alongside Amazon, Netflix, Lam Research and SoFi Technologies. Subsequent updates pushed the total number of objecting companies to 67 by today.

The original selection included 62 companies covering 63 proposed stock tickers. The latest tally therefore extends beyond the initial roster, with 56 original companies having filed objections.

Under the SEC’s temporary Innovation Exemption, trading venues must notify companies before offering third-party tokenised versions of their shares. Issuers can object within 30 days, preventing the venue from listing those particular tokenised shares.

Importantly, these objections do not represent a blanket rejection of tokenisation. Companies can still explore their own tokenisation arrangements or participate through other venues.

OKXICE tokenized stocks proposal uses permissioned liquidity pools on OKX’s X Layer blockchain, with Uniswap v4 infrastructure supporting trading. Investors would undergo identity and sanctions checks before accessing the platform.

The initiative aims to combine blockchain settlement with extended trading hours, although the growing number of objections raises questions about which major stocks could eventually become available.

Musk responded to Druckenmiller’s post on X with a single word: “Interesting.”

The announcement involved a separate ICE initiative designed to bring perpetual futures trading to the United States using Hyperliquid infrastructure. Under the proposed arrangement, ICE will operate the regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure, while Trade[XYZ] will develop the markets using Hyperliquid’s technology.

The platform intends to offer around-the-clock perpetual contracts linked to cryptocurrencies, equities, commodities, and foreign exchange. ICE is also making a strategic investment in Trade[XYZ], giving the agreement a direct institutional connection to the growing market for blockchain-based financial products.

#5519. Invitation Homes, HBI team up to train vets in skilled trades

Home Builders Institute and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership that channels Invitation Homes’ Invitation to SkillUp initiative into HBI’s Military Services program. The effort expands recruiting at HBI military sites such as Fort Stewart and Jacksonville and uses Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group for mentoring.  AI Summary

Invitation Homes and Home Builders Institute (HBI) have formed a partnership to expand training and job placement for transitioning armed services members, veterans and their families seeking careers in construction, property maintenance and other skilled trades, according to a company announcement.

The collaboration is part of Invitation Homes’ Invitation to SkillUp initiative and will support HBI’s Military Services program with hands-on, instructor-led training, industry-recognized certifications and job placement services.

Under the agreement, HBI and Invitation Homes plan to connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses and family members with roles in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors, expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida, and use Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group for mentorship and career guidance. The partners also aim to highlight success stories of veterans and family members who move into skilled trades careers.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes President and CEO Dallas Tanner said in the release. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI President and CEO Ed Brady said the nonprofit has spent the past decade training, certifying and placing transitioning military members, veterans and their families in skilled trades roles. Nearly 90% of its military program graduates secure jobs, earning on average more than three times the federal minimum wage, according to the announcement.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is the company’s national skilled trades development platform, which partners with trade schools and workforce organizations across the country to broaden access to skills education and promote trades careers.

Invitation Homes joins other national backers of HBI’s military programs, including The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT. A recent $1 million gift from Google, followed by the new investment from Invitation Homes, underscores rising industry interest in supporting veterans and their families in building long-term skilled trades careers.

For homebuilders, the partnership represents one more channel to address chronic labor shortages in residential construction and property maintenance by tapping into a pipeline of trained veterans at a time when the industry continues to struggle with aging trades workers and elevated repair and maintenance demand.

#5518. Diagrid’s Dapr 1.19 lightens AI agent workflows and drops a control-plane service

Agent infrastructure startup Diagrid Inc. today released Dapr 1.19 with changes that cut the overhead of the durable workflows behind long-running artificial intelligence agents.

Operators of the open-source runtime can also drop one of its control-plane services. Until 1.19, Dapr’s workflow engine shipped the entire execution history to the worker on every step.

Each one adds to that history. On a job that runs for hours or fans out into dozens of parallel tasks, the payload keeps growing, and Diagrid said that pushed up latency and memory use. Now a worker keeps what it already holds and gets only new events.

That makes the data sent per step independent of how long a workflow has been running. Workers still replay the full history locally. The smaller transfers go only to workers that advertise support for them, which in 1.19 means those built on Dapr’s Java and Python software development kits.

Mark Fussell, Diagrid’s co-founder and chief product officer, said an agent “that runs all afternoon and splits into 50 tasks can’t haul its entire history across the network on every step.”

A second workflow change, an opt-in preview feature called WorkflowsFastPath, stops pushing every workflow event through a durable scheduler reminder. Wake-ups and local activities are handled in place. The reminder path stays as a backstop for recovery, and in Diagrid’s engine benchmarks median step latency fell from 553 milliseconds to 153 milliseconds with the feature on.

Two services have made up Dapr’s control plane until now, and a new mode in 1.19 retires Placement, which distributes the actor placement table. The surviving Scheduler service handles jobs, reminders and workflow scheduling, and it already tracks cluster membership and pushes state to sidecars the same way Placement does.

Yaron Schneider, a co-creator of Dapr who is also Diagrid’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said the pair “matured as two services doing overlapping work.” With the mode on, the Scheduler takes over actor placement and the standalone Placement service is no longer deployed. That spares operators a stateful service and the Raft consensus cluster behind it. Reminders get faster too, because the Scheduler knows which sidecar owns each actor.

Scaling events are also less disruptive. A host joining or leaving used to pause placement across the entire namespace while Dapr re-sent its placement table. In the new mode, only the affected actor types are locked and updated, and the rest keep serving traffic.

New alpha building blocks in 1.19 are aimed at developers of AI applications. A Vector building block offers a portable application programming interface for storing and querying embeddings through similarity search, with Meilisearch as its first supported component.

Binary Store streams large files such as model outputs in chunks so they never have to sit in memory whole. Its first components cover Amazon S3 and the object stores from Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle.

Developers working in .NET get Actors.Next, a new actor SDK that generates proxies and registration code at compile time, which cuts runtime overhead and lets actor apps compile with Native AOT.

Dapr 1.19 is available now. WorkflowsFastPath ships turned off, and the Scheduler placement mode is enabled through a Helm setting once every sidecar runs 1.19, with no sidecar restart needed to switch it on or off. Teams running Dapr on Kubernetes can manage the upgrade through Diagrid’s Dapr Ops Dashboard, and the company said the tool typically supports new releases within 24 hours.

#5516. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5514. Broadcom open-sources its Kubernetes VM manager

Broadcom Inc. is contributing an open-source project for managing virtual machines with Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, part of an effort to simplify operations across increasingly diverse enterprise computing environments.

The company announced today that its VM application programming interface project has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, the entry point for early-stage cloud-native projects. VM API  provides a vendor-neutral framework for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same APIs that Kubernetes employs to orchestrate modular and portable software containers.

Broadcom also announced an initiative to standardize application behavior across Kubernetes distributions and expanded support for third-party software on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service.

The announcements, made at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect the growing need for infrastructure that can support traditional applications alongside modern containerized and artificial intelligence workloads.

Although Kubernetes has become the dominant platform for container orchestration, virtual machines remain central to enterprise computing. A Linux Foundation survey of 492 practitioners scheduled to be released today found that VMs account for 53% of production applications, with most respondents expecting that proportion to remain stable. Among organizations expanding their VM deployments, 34% cited AI and agentic workloads as contributing factors.

Broadcom’s VM API project addresses the operational complexity of managing VMs and containers separately. It uses Kubernetes’ declarative management model to create and manage virtual machines across different infrastructure providers while preserving capabilities such as hardware isolation and specialized input/output performance.

“We want to do the same thing now for virtual machines,” said Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, referring to Kubernetes’ existing Cluster API initiative.

The goal is to provide consistent management across environments without requiring organizations to abandon their existing virtualization investments.

“Ultimately, our goal is to make virtual machines first-class citizens of a Kubernetes environment without sacrificing what makes them distinct and valuable for our customers,” Shenoy said.

The project could also simplify operations for administrators accustomed to working with Kubernetes rather than maintaining separate management tools for virtualized and containerized infrastructure.

Broadcom’s second initiative addresses a different interoperability problem: inconsistent application behavior across Kubernetes distributions.

The company is co-chairing a newly established Workload Conformance Working Group to develop common expectations for how applications operate across Kubernetes environments.

Existing conformance programs verify that Kubernetes distributions support standard APIs, but that doesn’t guarantee applications will behave identically across platforms. Differences in infrastructure capabilities, configuration and operational practices can introduce incompatibilities.

“Just because two Kubernetes environments are conformant doesn’t necessarily mean that the application will behave consistently across both,” Shenoy said.

The proposed workload conformance standard would help software vendors reduce the need to certify applications separately for individual Kubernetes distributions while giving enterprises greater confidence in application portability.

Broadcom also announced more than 20 newly validated partner solutions for VKS, the Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation.

The validations span observability, security, data management, AI, application delivery, networking and storage. They are intended to help organizations deploy Kubernetes workloads using familiar third-party tools without requiring extensive integration or changes to existing operational practices.

Broadcom said its broader VKS ecosystem now includes more than 90 independent software vendors participating in testing and validation.

#5513. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5512. NAR moves from survival to ‘showing receipts’ on member value

NAR leaders used the 2026 NXT board meeting to outline year 1 of the 2026 to 2028 strategic plan. Updates included outreach to 450+ MLSs, Tuccori settlement participation, MLS policy changes, advocacy wins and education platform upgrades.  AI Summary

A little over two years have passed since Nykia Wright was named permanent CEO of the National Association of Realtors (NAR). Her tenure as the CEO of the nation’s largest trade association began in a period of unprecedented turmoil for the over 100 year old organization.

During an address to NAR’s board of directors Monday morning at NAR’s 2026 NXT conference and board meeting, Wright attributed much of the association’s success in navigating this turmoil to 2025 NAR President Kevin Sears, who began his term early, in January 2024 after Tracy Kasper’s resignation.

“I wanted to remind us just how much leadership matters. The two years of Kevin Sears’s leadership was defined by leading us through never before experienced turbulence,” Wright, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, said. “Not just the turbulence of survival versus extinction, which is singularly difficult on its own, but also cultural turbulence. And under his leadership, we set the groundwork for what we were promising we were going to do if we were given the chance.”

For the past year, however, it was 2026 NAR President Kevin Brown, who was tasked with carrying out the plan, namely the first year of NAR’s 2026-2028 strategic plan.

“Kevin Brown’s leadership was defined by the showing of actual receipts. January 1st of this year represented the official starting of the clock for our three-year strategic plan that was authored by the membership. They asked, and he began to deliver,” Wright said.

Under Brown’s guidance this year, Wright said that this was the first year NAR made contact with all 450+ MLSs across the country. In addition to this, NAR settled the homebuyer commission lawsuits by opting into the Tuccori settlement, which is awaiting final approval, added 30 new co-sponsors to the More Homes on the Market bill and the trade group implemented zero-based budgeting.

“I want to thank Kevin Brown and his leadership team for every single week continuing to hold us accountable, continuing to cross-examine our thinking, and for using every opportunity when he traveled across the country to bring back new and fresh feedback as we needed to be considered as we strive to continue to add value for our members,” Wright said.

In taking the helm from Sears last fall, Brown said his primary focus was on getting Realtors “back to business” by helping members “navigate the issues that impact their day-to-day business like financing, inventory, insurance, zoning restrictions and other barriers to home and property ownership.”

This translated into tackling a variety of challenges. Building off the changes approved last year, under Brown’s leadership NAR continued its work focused on supporting and strengthening MLS, but without trying to “run the MLS ecosystem.”

“We’ve strengthened the MLS collaboration through outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives, forming a new MLS work group to address emerging issues, help modernize the policies and shape resources and help members better serve clients and collect feedback to understanding the on-the-ground impact from members and the industry through surveys, focus groups, and in-person meetings,” Brown said.

These efforts came to fruition this week when the association approved four MLS policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee.

Beyond this, Brown aid NAR is working with federal lawmakers and MLS leaders on things like modernizing the copyright registration process, as well as advocating to antitrust regulators that the MLS helps increase competition in the brokerage space.

Brown also highlighted NAR’s advocacy wins this year, which included the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act and the expanded use of newer credit scoring models by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Housing Administration (FHA).

Looking ahead, Brown said NAR remains focused on the implementation of the ROAD Act and working on gaining more support for the More Homes on the Market Act, which would update the capital gains tax exclusion on the sale of a primary residence.

The past year also saw NAR work to improve  its education for agents, building a “unified education experience.” This included modernizing education classes, improving the quality of instructors and creating an improved digital learning experience with a new learning management platform.

“NAR is enhancing the Center for Realtor Development so we can raise the professionalism of our industry through education and provide better programs and resources members can use to get to their next transaction faster with greater confidence,” Brown said.

Finally, Brown noted NAR’s efforts to deepen its relationships with its brokers, expanding broker engagement and “turning direct broker input into dedicated programming, peer connections and business resources.”

“NAR is connected with more than 15,000 brokers through state and local brokers for summits. And we’re on track for participating in more than 85 broker summits by the end of the year,” Brown said. “We also organized the inaugural broker innovation forum here at NXT based on the success of the broker policy forum at the Realtors Legislative Meeting. The first broker mastermind event drew more than 460 participants to discuss, strengthen the talent pipeline, modernizing the brokers using AI and broker tech essentials.”

Brown said that this was clearly the type of content brokers found helpful and that positively contributed to their business.

As he departed the presidency, Brown thanked NAR’s advocacy team for all of their work this year, as well as the leadership team, staff and Wright.

“It has been an honor to represent NAR and serve as your 2026 president because each day Realtors work hard to make a positive difference and change people’s lives for the better. I’m proud to be a Realtor and I hope you are too. Let’s keep working together so we can continue making a difference for our communities, our organization and our industry.”

#5511. TEN Holdings Announces Closing of $2.0 Million Registered Direct Offering

NEW YORK, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD) (the "Company" or "TEN Holdings"), the technology company behind TEN, a Digital Experience Platform that powers the next generation of enterprise digital engagement, today announced the closing of its registered direct offering of an aggregate of 3,389,831 shares of the Company's common stock at a purchase price of $0.59 per share.

The gross proceeds from the offering were approximately $2.0 million, before deducting offering expenses payable by the Company.

The Company intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for working capital and general corporate purposes, supporting its ongoing operations and strategic initiatives as it continues its transition toward a technology-driven, recurring-revenue business model.

"This financing represents another important step in strengthening our financial position as we continue executing our long-term growth strategy," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings. "Over the past several months, we have made meaningful progress in reducing our operating cost structure, expanding our technology capabilities, and transitioning toward a more scalable SaaS business model. This additional capital will provide us with greater financial flexibility to support our operations and continue building on that momentum."

Mr. Torres added, "With our new TEN Digital Experience Platform launched and our focus increasingly shifting toward recurring software revenue, we believe we are entering an important phase in the Company's development. We remain committed to disciplined capital allocation, improving operational efficiency, and positioning TEN Holdings for sustainable long-term growth and shareholder value creation."

The shares of common stock were offered pursuant to an effective shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (File No. 333-299485), which was declared effective by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") on October 26, 2026. The offering was made only by means of a prospectus supplement and accompanying base prospectus. A prospectus supplement relating to the offering has been filed with the SEC and is available on the SEC's website at www.sec.gov.

This press release does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy any securities, nor shall there be any sale of securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD) is a New York-based technology company focused on developing enterprise software solutions that enable organizations to create, manage, deliver, and measure digital experiences. Through its flagship Digital Experience Platform, TEN, the Company provides technology solutions for enterprise communications, virtual events, webinars, and continuing education, supporting digital experiences with up to 50,000 concurrent attendees.

Building on more than a decade of experience serving Fortune 500 companies, TEN Holdings is evolving its platform into a broader, AI-enabled enterprise technology ecosystem. Its product roadmap includes marketing automation, CRM integrations, advanced engagement analytics, AI-powered capabilities, and content management solutions designed to help organizations streamline workflows, strengthen customer engagement, and generate actionable business insights.

The Company's strategy is centered on expanding its SaaS offerings, increasing recurring revenue opportunities, and delivering scalable technology solutions to enterprise customers. Planned capabilities remain subject to ongoing development, and there can be no assurance regarding their timing or availability.

#5510. Red Hat adds agentic AI operations, stronger security in OpenShift 5 and RHEL updates

Red Hat Inc. today announced a major update to its OpenShift Kubernetes-based application development platform that adds artificial intelligence-powered troubleshooting, stronger security controls and simplified upgrades as the company seeks to make its hybrid cloud infrastructure easier to manage.

The company also announced new versions of Red Hat Enterprise Linux with enhanced protection against software tampering, AI-assisted system administration and post-quantum cryptography.

The releases, unveiled at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect Red Hat’s continuing initiatives to embed AI into enterprise infrastructure management while strengthening security across increasingly distributed environments.

Red Hat OpenShift 5, the first major version upgrade in seven years, extends the platform’s ability to manage containers, virtual machines and AI workloads within a common environment. It also broadens the OpenShift Lightspeed generative AI assistant into an agent capable of investigating operational problems and recommending corrective actions.

“It’s infusing intelligence into the platform with agent-based troubleshooting through a simple interface with Lightspeed and natural language,” said Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer and senior vice president of global engineering.

The updated Lightspeed interface allows administrators to generate visualizations of system performance using natural-language requests. For example, an administrator can ask for central processing unit utilization over the previous week, add memory consumption and overlay application errors. The resulting charts can be saved to dashboards that update continuously.

More significantly, OpenShift 5 introduces agentic troubleshooting that automatically investigates cluster events. When problems occur, the system can examine related information, reason through possible causes and propose remediation steps. Administrators retain control over whether the recommended actions are executed.

The platform also includes an AI-driven upgrade planner that examines application dependencies, Kubernetes application programming interfaces and optional operators to identify potential compatibility problems before updates begin.

“It is easy to upgrade Kubernetes,” said Mike Barrett, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager of hybrid cloud platforms. “What is difficult is navigating all the things you’re running on top of Kubernetes.”

Security enhancements include hardened multitenancy, more extensive network isolation, automated certificate management and post-quantum cryptography for control-plane communications. The capabilities are aimed in part at sovereign cloud providers and regulated organizations that must maintain strict separation between tenants and demonstrate compliance with security requirements.

OpenShift 5 also supports automated graphics processing unit resource allocation across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads, potentially improving utilization of that expensive computing infrastructure.

Unlike previous major platform transitions, OpenShift 5 can be installed as an in-place update from OpenShift 4, avoiding the need to reinstall software or migrate workloads, Red Hat said. A revised lifecycle approach provides greater predictability for customers operating long-lived enterprise applications and virtualized infrastructure.

“We are no longer asking you to reinstall or migrate to use more of our product,” Barrett said. “This is a simple upgrade.”

The company is emphasizing virtualization as an increasingly important part of its business. Barrett said OpenShift Virtualization has grown to an $800 million business as customers seek alternatives to traditional virtualization platforms.

It said NASA’s laboratory migrated approximately 2,400 virtual machines to OpenShift Virtualization, while Gates Corp. moved more than 1,300 virtual machines and reported a 50% increase in available compute capacity.

The forthcoming Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.3 and 9.9 releases extend the company’s security strategy to the operating system.

A principal addition in RHEL 10.3 is support for sealed images, which use customer-controlled cryptographic keys to verify operating system integrity from the bootloader through the kernel and root file system. The technology is designed to prevent unauthorized modifications and block compromised software components from running.

Red Hat is also introducing a Model Context Protocol server that allows compatible AI assistants to investigate live Linux systems while maintaining access controls. Integration with Performance Co-Pilot, an open-source toolkit for monitoring, recording, analyzing, and controlling infrastructure, enables agents to examine historical performance information alongside current system conditions to identify the causes of operational problems.

A self-managed version of the RHEL command-line assistant, available in developer preview, lets organizations run AI inference locally. The capability is intended for disconnected, air-gapped and regulated environments where sending operational information outside the organization may be prohibited.

The releases also introduce post-quantum cryptography support for applications built using the Go programming language, including integration of the post-quantum Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism encryption algorithm with the language’s Transport Layer Security implementation. Additional enhancements include updated developer toolchains and support for newer processor architectures.

Red Hat separately announced Developer Hub 2.1, an update to its enterprise developer portal that gives AI coding agents governed access to organizational information, approved software components and standardized development workflows. Through MCP integration, agents can discover existing services, follow established development procedures and perform authorized actions using enterprise tooling.

The update also introduces expanded AI asset cataloging, a context-aware assistant and a longer support lifecycle, increasing the release support window from six to 10 months. Developer Hub 2.1 is generally available, as is OpenShift 5, while the new RHEL versions are expected in the coming weeks.

#5509. What View Homes’ rebrand says about Gandhi’s operating overhaul

View Homes is consolidating its regional brands into a single identity as CEO Natasha Gandhi works to standardize operating practices and data systems. The company is expanding in Colorado and assessing how Hunt’s new Strata platform could support land strategy.  AI Summary

Seven months into her effort to transform View Homes from a loose collection of regional builders into a cohesive enterprise, CEO Natasha Gandhi has drawn a line between the company’s past and its ambitions.

A newly unified brand makes that promise visible. Now Gandhi and her team must overdeliver on it.

View Homes announced Monday a new corporate brand identity, unifying its formerly distinct Aspen View, Desert View, Horizon View and View Homes operations under one name. The change spans five divisions across Colorado, New Mexico and Texas and marks a milestone in the operational transformation Gandhi began after becoming CEO in March 2026.

The announcement also comes one week after View’s parent, Hunt Companies, joined with global investment manager Wafra to launch Strata Land Partners, a new land-financing platform led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum. Together, these developments offer a clearer view of Hunt’s expanding ambitions in U.S. residential construction and development.

In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD, Gandhi said the branding initiative is part of a broader effort to prepare View for growth, strengthen operating standards, and compete across more markets and homebuyer segments.

“We want to be a premium builder, and by premium, it’s not that we’re unaffordable,” Gandhi said. “It just means that we want to be the best in every price point that we’re out there, we want to be the best in every market that we build in.”

Hunt acquired full ownership of View Homes in 2025, inheriting an established 35-year-old homebuilding business whose regional operations had developed distinct identities, systems and operating practices.

When Gandhi arrived in March, she found an organization with strong local relationships and experienced teams, but lacking the consistent management processes, reporting systems, and enterprise infrastructure needed to support the growth Hunt envisioned.

As The Builder’s Daily reported in October, Gandhi’s initial work focused on leadership changes, clearer accountability, more disciplined sales concessions, selective land investment, and a comprehensive review of enterprise technology.

The new branding establishes four standards intended to apply across the organization: exceptional customer experience, people-first leadership, design-forward homes, and premium quality across price points.

“I felt like previously, we had different standards in different markets, but now with this new brand, it really sets the stage,” Gandhi said. “These four pillars are something that is now going to be operationally executed in all our markets.”

The challenge is to translate those commitments into consistent performance without compromising the local knowledge and customer relationships that have made View’s regional businesses successful.

For a multiregional homebuilder, Gandhi notes, that means more than consistent signage and marketing. It requires shared expectations for product quality, customer service, sales execution, and management accountability, supported by reliable information and operating systems.

Gandhi is candid that the transformation remains unfinished. “This is just the start of our growth journey,” she said. “I will tell you, we’re not there yet, but we’re on the path of getting there.”

The branding initiative has prompted further scrutiny of the operational capabilities needed to support the company’s ambitions to up its game. Gandhi acknowledged that View’s enterprise resource planning systems and website are not yet up to par.

A builder seeking to expand across markets needs timely, consistent information on sales, margins, construction costs, inventory, and land commitments. Without it, management cannot easily compare performance across divisions or make informed decisions about capital allocation.

Gandhi previously outlined a 12-to-18-month enterprise technology implementation, along with efforts to standardize sales concessions and improve the quality of operating data. Those initiatives remain important to the company’s ability to scale.

View has also raised the bar in its home merchandising across markets and is developing products designed to reach beyond its traditional entry-level customer base. The objective is to preserve affordability where that remains the market opportunity while broadening View’s appeal to move-up buyers and customers seeking greater design and product differentiation.

The transformation is unfolding amid difficult housing economics. Slower sales, persistent affordability pressures, and costly incentives continue to strain builder margins, while land acquisition and development require substantial capital commitments long before homes generate revenue.

Hunt’s ownership gives View access to a larger real estate investment organization and a longer-term investment perspective. Its recent partnership with Wafra to establish Strata Land Partners adds another potentially valuable capability.

Strata launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land-financing solutions for public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide. Forsum has described the platform as a capital partner “built by builders, for builders,” emphasizing the need to understand the operational risks and financial requirements of homebuilding businesses.

Gandhi confirmed that View and Strata are already discussing opportunities to work together.

“We are actually already exploring opportunities to where Strata and [View] can partner together,” she said. “There’s definitely opportunity and conversations already in place.”

She did not identify specific transactions or financing structures under review.

Still, the potential relationship illustrates how Hunt’s residential investments could create complementary advantages. View brings homebuilding operations, local market relationships, and demand for future lots. Strata brings a platform designed to finance land acquisition and development while managing builders’ capital exposure.

Whether those capabilities translate into direct financial or operational advantages for View will depend on the transactions and terms the companies ultimately pursue. Strata’s mandate extends well beyond Hunt-owned businesses.

Gandhi said she has assembled the leadership team she believes can execute View’s next phase, including experienced executives recruited during the restructuring process.

“It’s your people that get you the results,” she said. “It’s your people that help you navigate a tough market.”

That leadership investment comes as View prepares to expand into Sterling Ranch, a master-planned community in Douglas County, Colorado, near Denver.

View currently operates in Northern Colorado, Colorado Springs, and Las Cruces, El Paso, and San Antonio. Sterling Ranch gives the company an opportunity to establish a stronger presence in the Denver metropolitan market, where Gandhi sees additional growth opportunities.

She said View is close to completing other land transactions in the Denver area and is pursuing opportunities in additional master-planned communities.

The expansion also offers an early test of the unified brand’s positioning. View intends to compete as a premium regional builder while maintaining a product range that serves buyers across price points.

Gandhi’s transformation is underway as many homebuilders protect cash, reduce land commitments, and prepare for the possibility that difficult conditions could persist through 2027 and 2028. View must balance those immediate pressures with Hunt’s longer-term objective of building a substantially larger homebuilding enterprise.

The company is not simply adding communities to its existing business. Gandhi is working to establish the leadership, systems, product standards, and capital discipline needed to support growth without replicating the fragmented operating structure she inherited.

“My goal, Hunt’s goal, is for View to grow into a premium regional builder,” Gandhi said. “I would like to see View be among the top 50, top 25 home builders in the next five years.”

Achieving that scale will require more than additional land and investment capital. View must demonstrate that its five divisions can operate consistently, protect margins amid changing market conditions, and deliver – or exceed – the customer experience its new brand promises.
